TR DECISION MAKING / VIRTUAL CLASSROOM PREFACE INSTRUCTOR / PRODUCER GUIDE

# Preface

Course Goal By the end of the course, learners will be able to make decisions on TR applications (visitors, international students, and temporary workers) consistent with the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) and the relevant Program Delivery Instructions (PDI)

Prerequisites In this course, the learners build on what they have learned earlier in Introduction to Decision Making (CC8307), e-Introduction to Immigration (CC8200), and Inadmissibility in IRPA (CC7700). To successfully participate in the virtual learning sessions, we recommend that learners take the IRCC Learning Academy course “Getting Ready to Learn in the Virtual Classroom”.

Approach This course combines self-directed learning (eWorkbook and exercise booklet), and group learning (virtual classroom sessions). Learners will complete the content of the eWorkbook and exercise booklet independently, and join the group learning as per the schedule. Scenario reading is required in preparation of each group learning session. These scenarios are included in the participant's guide. The eWorkbook provides the course's informational content. During the group learning sessions, learners practice the concepts learned independently. That is why understanding the importance of self-directed learning is essential for successful participation in the group learning and for course learning outcomes.

Unit 2 Visitor Applications In Unit 2, visitors, you will learn about foreign nationals who require temporary 昆 Unit 3 resident visas, electronic travel authorizations, visitor records and much more! Producer: Share the eWorkbook on the screen and show an exercise. Next, show the exercise booklet.

Instructor:

Explain how to work with the eWorkbook and exercise booklet. Demonstrate by showing: topic, hyperlinked references and related activity. Then demonstrate the corresponding activity in the exercise booklet where they complete their responses. Also be sure to mention that the eWorkbook contains tagged that are specific for each network and that learners do not need to complete the exercises for the other networks.

“1. Read a topic in your eWorkbook, then read the instruction for the exercise. Both legislative and PDI references have been provided to support your learning. Let's look at an example.

2. To complete the exercises, go to your exercise booklet. There, you can write down your answers for practice activities and make your notes. Some exercises contain scenarios that are designated with an asterisk (*) which means that those are optional for extra practice. We recommend keeping your exercise booklet open while working with the eWorkbook. You do not have to submit the exercise booklet to your instructor, it is provided to you for your own practice. To make the exercise booklet interactive, enable macros by clicking Enable Content button when you open the exercise booklet. Where applicable, both legislative and PDI references have also been provided to support the activities. Let's look at an example.

NOTE: When assessing dual intent, an officer should distinguish between temporary residence applicants whose intention to fulfill their obligations as a temporary resident (to leave at the end of their period of authorized stay as required by section (R179) is bona fide and an applicant who has no intention of leaving Canada at the end of their authorized stay. ### Questions Answers

Scenario 4 Ganish received a refusal letter following his request to extend his visitor status in Canada for an additional six months. He arrived in Canada in December and was given a six-month visitor record expiring in June. He applied to extend his status in July but was refused for the sole reason of having lost his status as per A47(a). Following his refusal letter, Ganish sent in an application to restore his status as a visitor and supporting documents demonstrating his ability to support himself as he would like to remain in Canada to continue his journey towards the East Coast. He explained that he was in the Canadian Rockies at the time his status expired and was unable to access the Internet to send his online application.

# KeyLost status as per A47(a)

## Factors

Applied within 90 days following the refusal of his application considered Does he meet the requirements of R182(1)

## Decision Approve

Ganish lost his status as per A47(a) because he did not apply to extend his status prior to the end of the period for which they are authorized to remain in Canada. Although he was refused, he applied to restore his status within the 90 days after he lost his temporary resident status. NOTE: If an application for an extension of temporary resident status under section R181 is refused, the foreign national has 90 days from the date of losing temporary resident status, if otherwise eligible. If an application for an extension is received after the temporary resident status is lost, the case processing centre should refuse the application and respond with a warning notice to the applicant that they are eligible to apply for restoration.

### TR DECISION MAKING / VIRTUAL CLASSROOM

UNIT 2: VISITOR APPLICATIONS INSTRUCTOR / PRODUCER GUIDE

Activity: Credibility Credibility comprises the objective and subjective components of the believability of a foreign national and the documents submitted in support of an application. In the Introduction to Decision Making course as well as in the Inadmissibility Curriculum, officers learned that a part of the assessment of a file, could include a further review of the evidence (i.e. documents, statements) in relation to its reliability and trustworthiness.

### The class will be divided into groups.

The scenarios contain a background of the case and initial assessment of the documents. This is an opportunity to discuss the evidence as a group and identify possible concerns with the case. Allotted time: 20 minutes

Scenario 1: Radbod has submitted a second application to extend their visitor status. Initial reasons and first extension related to visiting relatives. Radbod has been in Canada for one year and is now requesting for an extension to visit his girlfriend. A review of the edoc file has raised concerns.

## Evidence Observations

Address history Girlfriend's address since entry to Canada

## Financial statementsContinual cash deposits every 2-3 weeks estimating $500-$700 for the past 3 months

GCMS information on girlfriendThe girlfriend submitted a previous spousal sponsorship application two years ago that was refused. The application was for the sponsorship of a different person than the foreign national in question.

# Address historyGirlfriend's address since entry to Canada

Concerns

Current activities-intended to visit family but has been staying with a girlfriend who was not mentioned upon entry and previous extension request Finances – concerned regarding the source of cash deposits (possibly working in Canada) Relationship with girlfriend- intentions with relationship as no details regarding relationship itself was mentioned previously Integrated search on girlfriend shows she tried to sponsor a spouse before -is she still married, reasons for divorce, etc.

Scenario 2: Rochelle has submitted an application for a visitor record extension to visit Canadian citizen son in Cavendish, Prince Edward Island. Rochelle has been in Canada for the past two years. She has received one extension and has maintained her status. Rochelle wants to continue her stay in Canada to help with her son and future daughter-in-law's wedding planning and to be there for this milestone. The wedding will take place in a few months. You review bank statements showing regular monthly pension deposits but for the past eight months there are biweekly deposits between $200 and $300. You see an Info Alert that describes work without authorization allegations. The Info Alert is a letter describing that Rochelle is working as a personal support worker for an elderly neighbour. The letter further outlines Rochelle's job duties and that the neighbour pays her a mix of cash and e-transfers. A review of the edoc file has raised concerns.

# Concerns

Possibly working without authorization and misrepresentation-affects the credibility of the foreign national for not disclosing employment and/or having sufficient funds for stay in Canada (bank deposits-monthly pension with recent biweekly deposits).

# 10.0 Debriefing on Credibility (15 minutes)

Instructor:

Refer to Activity: Credibility to review the scenario with the learners and comment accordingly. “Let's listen to your presentations and discuss the scenarios together. Whose group is going to present first?” Please raise your hands.

Discuss the learners' comments, and provide examples when needed. Reiterate to participants that credibility has to do with the veracity, usually of the person, but could be applied to a document. Reliability is maybe closer to accuracy, neutrality etc. You could therefore have a credible applicant that provides information that is not reliable. The term credibility is best used where one would not believe something because it is possibly a lie, fraud or misrepresentation. Whenever the applicant's credibility or the credibility of their documents is in question, it is imperative that procedural fairness is engaged by providing the applicant the opportunity to respond by sending a Procedural Fairness Letter or through an interview. It is not generally necessary to proceed with procedural fairness for information that is unreliable, but it is necessary to proceed with procedural fairness if there are credibility concerns.

Ask whether the learners have any questions. Answer their questions and elaborate on details when needed. Advise learners, references will be included in the answer key.

Transition to the next topic. “In your workbooks, you learned that there are two components that are reviewed in every application: (1) eligibility and (2) admissibility. We just finished examining the eligibility requirements and also reviewed the topic of credibility. If there are no questions at this point, we will now move onto the next component and learn about inadmissibility”.

1. Explain to the learners that you are going to show and read a multi-part scenario out to them. Each part will introduce incremental changes in the circumstances of the applicants. At each development, they need to “take a stand" on their decision on the case by using the pointer tool from the annotation toolbar and by clicking in the approve, refuse or refer column.
2.It is not incorrect to say that answers may vary, for example where officers must be satisfied on balance of probabilities (ex.: R179(b)). ## Questions Answers

Scenario 2 Mohammed recently graduated from with a diploma in Business Administration. He is now requesting a study permit to attend He provided an LOA with a scholarship valued at $5,000. The applicant provided bank statements, transcripts from proof of program completion, lease agreement and a valid passport. Cross-reference shows that applicant's accompanying spouse has not applied for an extension to their visitor record. Visitor record expired last month. No information provided to indicate spouse left Canada. Bank statement is a joint account with spouse.

# KeyLOA for new school

Factors Logical progression of studies considered Funds – scholarship, joint account with spouse

Decision 1. Approve. Despite concerns with accompanying spouse, sufficient evidence provided to satisfy R217 for this application. Continual pursuit of business degree. Although funds are from joint account, partial scholarship and foreign national has the ability to work part-time on-campus and off-campus.

2. Refer the file for further review regarding spouse's intention to remain in Canada. Funds are from joint account with spouse. However, applicant would not be an inadmissible family member as per A42(1). NOTE: A42(1) inadmissibility applies only when a foreign national applying for temporary residence has a family member who is inadmissible under A34, A35 or A37, whether the family member is accompanying the foreign national or not.

Scenario 5 Melania recently graduated from with a nursing degree. Requesting a study permit to further her nursing studies in the Psychiatric Nursing program. Provided a LOA and bank statements, transcripts from her nursing degree, proof of program completion, lease agreement and a valid passport. Cross-reference shows accompanying spouse has not applied for an extension to their visitor record. No information provided to indicate spouse left Canada. Bank statement is a joint account with spouse. Visitor record expired last month.

If inadmissible, cite the Not inadmissible, A42 of spouse does not apply. reference. If not inadmissible, explain why.

## DecisionApprove. Despite concerns with accompanying spouse, sufficient evidence provided to satisfy R217 for this

application. NOTE: A42(1) inadmissibility applies only when a foreign national applying for temporary residence has a family member who is inadmissible under A34, A35 or A37, whether the family member is accompanying the foreign national or not.

## TR Decision Making

# How to use the Participant Guide

The Participant Guide contains scenarios that you will work on during the group learning sessions. For better learning experience, we recommend reading the scenarios and making your notes before the group learning session. During the virtual or classroom sessions, you will have opportunities to participate in group discussions and activities, ask questions, and benefit from exchange with your peers and instructors. The Participant Guide also contains handouts for the presentations that will be displayed to you at the sessions. Answers to the scenarios will be sent to you after the sessions by email.

## Objective

At the end of this virtual session, you will be able to make decisions on visitor applications consistent with the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) and the relevant Program Delivery Instructions (PDI).

Section 1.0 – Eligibility (short scenarios)

- List the key factors considered.
- Based on the information, what is your decision? Explain.

## Section 3.0 – Credibility

Credibility comprises the objective and subjective components of the believability of a foreign national and the documents submitted in support of an application. In the Introduction to Decision Making course as well as in the Inadmissibility Curriculum, officers learned that a part of the assessment of a file, could include a further review of the evidence (i.e. documents, statements) in relation to its reliability and trustworthiness. The class will be divided into groups. The scenarios contain a background of the case and initial assessment of the documents. This is an opportunity to discuss the evidence as a group and identify possible concerns with the case. Allotted time: 20 minutes

DecisionRefuse-R179(b). Other than having a relationship with a Canadian, no supporting documents relating to funds / employment and intentions for a one-year extension. Refer-for further review of dual intent. NOTE: When assessing dual intent, an officer should distinguish between temporary residence applicants whose intention to fulfill their obligations as a temporary resident (to leave at the end of their period of authorized stay as required by section (R179) is bona fide and an applicant who has no intention of leaving Canada at the end of their authorized stay. In assessing the applicant's intentions, the individual circumstances of the temporary residence applicant must be examined; refusals of non-bona fide temporary residents may only withstand legal challenge when the refusal is based on the information related to the specific application before an officer.

# TR Decision Making

## Questions Answers

Scenario 4 Ganish received a refusal letter following his request to extend his visitor status in Canada for an additional six months. He arrived in Canada in December and was given a six-month visitor record expiring in June. He applied to extend his status in July but was refused for the sole reason of having lost his status as per A47(a). Following his refusal letter, Ganish sent in an application to restore his status as a visitor and supporting documents demonstrating his ability to support himself as he would like to remain in Canada to continue his journey towards the East Coast. He explained that he was in the Canadian Rockies at the time his status expired and was unable to access the Internet to send his online application.

# KeyLost status as per A47(a) Factors

Applied within 90 days following the refusal of his application considered

- Does he meet the requirements of R182(1)
## Decision Approve

Ganish lost his status as per A47(a) because he did not apply to extend his status prior to the end of the period for which they are authorized to remain in Canada. Although he was refused, he applied to restore his status within the 90 days after he lost his temporary resident status. NOTE: If an application for an extension of temporary resident status under section R181 is refused, the foreign national has 90 days from the date of losing temporary resident status, if otherwise eligible. If an application for an extension is received after the temporary resident status is lost, the case processing centre should refuse the application and respond with a warning notice to the applicant that they are eligible to apply for restoration.

Scenario 2A family of four submitted an application to extend their visitor status to continue visiting Canada. The family now plans to participate in Adventures by Disney Canadian Rockies 7-day tour and would like to stay for another six months. Proof of purchase of the tour for the family of four (approximately $20K USD). Both parents are neurosurgeons and have travelled to Canada several times within the last 10 years. ## Factorsreturned to their home country

considered No adverse information Purpose of travel is reasonable Expiry date of passports

## Decision Approve

As passports will be expiring in a little over three months, the visitor records would be issued for a period no more than three months. Scenario 2

Rochelle has submitted an application for a visitor record extension to visit Canadian citizen son in Cavendish, Prince Edward Island. Rochelle has been in Canada for the past two years. She has received one extension and has maintained her status. Rochelle wants to continue her stay in Canada to help with her son and future daughter-in-law's wedding planning and to be there for this milestone. The wedding will take place in a few months.

You review bank statements showing regular monthly pension deposits but for the past eight months there are biweekly deposits between $200 and $300. You see an Info Alert that describes work without authorization allegations. The Info Alert is a letter describing that Andrea is working as a personal support worker for an elderly neighbour. The letter further outlines Rochelle's job duties and that the neighbour pays her a mix of cash and e-transfers. A review of the edoc file has raised concerns.

Concemns

Possibly working without authorization and misrepresentation-affects the credibility of the foreign national for not disclosing employment and/or having sufficient funds for stay in Canada (bank deposits-monthly pension with recent biweekly deposits).

Scenario 3 Fatma is visiting her spouse who has been in Canada for two years on a four-year study permit. Fatma's visitor status will expire within one month as she only received six months visitor status because she told the POE and overseas office that her intention was to come to Canada to visit her spouse and return home after one month based on her vacation leave from work. She is requesting for an extension to her visitor record to coincide with the two years remaining duration of her spouse's study permit. No indication from her employer that she has received an extension to her leave. Info Alert noted applicant was refused entry to the US last month. The applicant did not disclose US refusal. Insufficient proof of funds provided to support both Fatma and her husband while they remain in Canada. She provided a letter addressing why she wants to remain in Canada as she has limited family back home, has no intention to work in Canada as she has minimal English language skills, husband will provide support as he works part-time at a grocery store (off-campus employment).

File referred for further review.

Scenario 2 Reem, a 76-year-old foreign national is requesting another extension of their stay for one year. They are visiting their PR child in Canada. The applicant provided supporting documents such as recently issued medical insurance issued valid for one year up to $50,000, proof of funds and proof of relationship. In the first extension, applicant was requested to undergo medicals. Medical file shows the applicant was requested for further medical examination as there is an issue with the kidneys. ## TR Decision Making

# Section 6.0 – Performance Activity Steps Descriptions / Answers

Background information Poonam and her spouse entered Canada on TRVs in which Poonam was approved as a clergy leader [R186(l)] for a gurdwara in Claresholm, Alberta. There were given one-year visitor status. In their TRV application, a letter from the gurdwara in Canada outlined the duties for providing spiritual counselling and functions relating to the gathering of the congregation while the letter from home gurdwara confirmed position in their ministry. Poonam and her spouse intended to come to Canada for one year. It was also noted the couple has had work related travels across the country and the couple has no dependents.

Step 1Their permits are about to expire so they are asking for one-year extension. Poonam explained both her and her husband are still needed in their temple. She continues with her spiritual duties while her spouse continues to do community service in the gurdwara. Accommodations and living expenses continue to be provided by the gurdwara.

Supporting factors Maintained status No concerns regarding gurdwara

Decision Approve-satisfied still meets R186(1)

Step 2Poonam and her spouse are applying for another extension. The letter from the gurdwara now states the congregation is in need of all its members to do extra work this year as volunteers have declined. Along with their spiritual counselling duties they were asked to take on extra responsibilities of teaching classes 2-3 times per week and managing the kitchen meal rotations.

Supporting Factors Maintained status No concerns regarding gurdwara Extra duties appear to be short-term and in response to a volunteer decline

Concerns Need to confirm specifics of extra duties as teaching classes and managing the kitchen are not covered under R186(1) but rather under LMIA exemption R205(d)

# Key Points ExerciseLearing

Academy Question 4 of 10 Answer:

We learned that paragraph R7(2) lists those that are exempt from the requirement to obtain a TRV. What do these foreign nationals, unless exempted, need to have if they are seeking to enter Canada by Air?

If a foreign national is exempt from obtaining a TRV, they are required to obtain an eTA R7.1(1). R7.1 (2) or 7.1(3) identifies those that are exempt from obtaining an eTA.

It is also important to remember that an eTA is required for those travelling to Canada by air and not by land, sea, or by rail. VISITOR APPLICATIONS – TR DECISION MAKING | Visual Aid 05 (cont) A-2021-22877-000256

# Key Points

As per R9(1), all foreign nationals are required to obtain a study permit for engaging in academic, professional, vocational or other education or training that is more than six months in duration at a DLI in Canada, unless exempted

A foreign national is exempt from a study permit requirement if they are described as being authorized to study without the issuance of a study permit in R188 or A30(2)

A foreign national can apply for a study permit before entry, on entry or after entry (R213, R214 and R215)

To be eligible for a study permit, a foreign national needs to meet the general requirements for all temporary residents R179 as well as the specific requirements of R216 or R217

A study permit cannot be issued without LOA or conditional LOA R219(1), unless exempted under R219(2) Students may be eligible to work on R186(f) or off campus R186(v) and be part of other work programs. Only full-time students can work on or off campus.

# Preface

Welcome to Temporary Resident Decision Making exercise booklet! Practice activities are an important part of the TR Decision Making course. This booklet will help you to apply what you have learned in the eWorkbook through practice. Here, you will find quests and exercises from the eWorkbook together with some reflective activities. Use the exercise booklet to:

- write down your answers for exercises
- reflect on your learning
- take notes and write down your questions

How to Complete the Exercise Booklet

We recommend keeping your exercise booklet open at the same time as you learn with the eWorkbook. When you see a reference to an exercise in the eWorkbook, go to the same exercise in the exercise booklet and write down your answers. Check your answers with the answer keys in the eWorkbook. Please complete all practice activities to be better prepared for the virtual or classroom sessions. Remember: If you need more information, you can always email your instructor or ask a question at a virtual or classroom session. Navigation For the most part, navigating through exercise booklet is similar to any other electronic document. Just like the eWorkbook, this booklet includes external and internal hyperlinks.

Keep in mind that to meet the requirements of R181(2) and get an extension of their authorization to remain in Canada as a TR, the foreign national must continue to meet the requirements of R179, including R179(b). You therefore have to be satisfied that they:

- will leave Canada at the end of the authorized stay

She states in her application that her parents are wiring her another $750 (CAD) and that the money should arrive “any day now". The address given on her application is the Vancouver Youth Hostel on Barrette Street. Esther indicates she has resided there since her arrival. # Preface

## Welcome to the Temporary Resident Decision Making course!

Prerequisites To successfully complete this eWorkbook, you must have completed: Introduction to Decision Making (CC8307) e-Introduction to Immigration (CC8200) Inadmissibility in IRPA (CC7700) Getting Ready to Learn in a Virtual Classroom (CC6520)

We are delighted to welcome you to your core training to become an effective officer assessing temporary resident (TR) applications. In this course, you will build on what you learned earlier in Introduction to Decision Making, e-Introduction to Immigration, and Inadmissibility in IRPA. You will get to practice making decisions and delve deeper into the TR requirements through case studies and exercises.

A group of subject matter experts, including representatives from the International (IN), Domestic (DN) and Centralized (CN) networks, Immigration Program Guidance (IPG), Case Management Branch (CMB) and Operations Planning and Performance Branch (OPPB) worked collaboratively with IRCC's Learning Academy to develop this course to support you in your work.

Whether you work in Canada (at a case processing centre or an IRCC local office), or at an office outside Canada, you will find the content of this course relevant to your job. That is because we apply the same Act, Regulations, and guidelines. Albeit differences exist depending on the roles and responsibilities of your office. For that, you will find specific notes and activities in this eWorkbook.

About practice activities This eWorkbook is designed to encourage active learning. Where information exists, such as manuals, policies and functional

Questions are reflective activities that help you to review your prior knowledge or knowledge of the course material. You do not have to write down your answers. Answers to the scenarios will be sent to you after the group learning sessions.

# TR Decision Making

# 1. Making Decisions on Temporary Resident Applications

Your role as an officer may be to make decisions on applications for clients outside of Canada or for clients in Canada. You may be responsible for issuing a Temporary Resident Visa (TRV), and/or an electronic Travel Authorization (eTA) to foreign nationals outside Canada, or to authorize or extend periods for authorized visits, study or work for persons in Canada.

When assessing TR applications, you must be satisfied that the foreign national meets the requirements and is not inadmissible to Canada. Some requirements are general and applicable to all classes of TR applications (visitors, students, workers), while others are specific to each class. For example, all TR applicants must have a valid travel document, however, only students are required to provide a letter of acceptance (LOA). In this section, you will review your role in the decision-making process.

## 1.1. Legislative Instruments

As you learned in the e-Introduction to Immigration course, there are three main classes of TR's: visitors, students, and temporary workers. In each of the following three units, you will delve into the requirements for each class, and practice making decisions.

The classes and the corresponding requirements come from the legislative documents guiding the Immigration programs: the IRPA and the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR). The instruments of Delegation and Designation identify who has the authority to make what type of decisions.

The operational guidance and instructions to process TR applications are elaborated in PDIs, Program Delivery Updates (PDUs), Operational Bulletins (OBs) and Operational Reminders (ORs).

Program Delivery Instructions (PDis) are official operational instructions released by IRCC. They provide the most up-to-date guidance for processing applications. They help ensure consistent processing and program delivery. The PDIs aim to help officers interpret acts and regulations.

## Program Delivery Updates (PDUs) are brief announcements to highlight updates to official IRCC PDIs.

Operational Bulletins (OBs) are updates to manual only if a manual has not yet been modernized to PDI format, or for one time emergency instructions for operational readiness.

|11

A-2021-22877-000553

Immigration, Réfugié 1*1and Cizenship Canadaet Citoyenneté Can Information disclosed under the Access to Information Act L'information divulguée en vertu de la toi sur l’accès à Tinfor

## TR Decision Making

2.1. Case Management Branch Case Management Branch (CMB) provides direction, support, and decision-making on complex, high-profile, sensitive and/or contentious immigration, citizenship and passport cases. CMB is also responsible for managing litigation and applying the Employer Compliance Regime by conducting desk inspections. CMB generally reaches out to managers regarding specific cases. An example would be a case from the minister's office. Your manager could assign you one of these cases and you would work with CMB on the file. For more information, refer to Handling high-profile, complex, sensitive or contentious cases.
2.2. Client Experience Branch The Client Experience Branch (CEB) is a centre of expertise dedicated to understanding and improving the client experience. From time to time you may receive requests from CEB. For example, they may ask you to provide an update on a client's file, or if a client is asking for a reconsideration to a negative decision you have made.
2.3. Immigration Program Guidance Branch Immigration Program Guidance Branch (IPG) provides direction on all aspects of immigration programs, domestically and internationally. Before speaking with your supervisor on sending a request for functional guidance, you should go through all available resources (i.e. PDI, manuals, bulletins, IRPA, etc.).
2.4. Integrity Risk Management Branch Integrity Risk Management Branch (IRMB) is responsible for ensuring the integrity of IRCC's programs and service delivery under the responsibility of the Operations Sector.
2.5. Migration Health Branch Migration Health Branch (MHB) is the centre of expertise for the management of health-related aspects of migration. They deliver health screening and related services under the authority of the IRPA, and deliver the Interim Federal Health Program.

4.2. Unreliable Travel Documents The lack or inconsistent use of security features on travel documents, as well as concerns with the process to produce and issue travel documents, can result in situations in which a document is considered insufficiently resistant to counterfeiting and fraudulent use. Such documents threaten the safety and security of Canadians as well as the integrity of the immigration system. As per R50.1, the Minister may designate certain travel documents as unreliable. IRCC maintains a public list identifying unreliable travel documents that do not meet the requirements of_R50(1) or R52(1). The following are not considered travel documents for the purposes ofR50(1) or R52(1):
- any passport issued by Somalia
- non-machine readable passports issued by the Czech Republic
- temporary passports issued by the Republic of South Africa
- provisional passports issued by Venezuela

5. Biometrics Biometrics are the measurement of unique physical characteristics. They significantly reduce the chance that one individual could pose as, or be mistaken for, another and fingerprints are screened against the national repository of criminal records. Their collection aids in deterring, detecting and stopping the entry of those who pose a risk to the health, safety and security of Canadians. They are also a reliable and accurate tool for establishing identity. Biometrics collection allows the Government of Canada to effectively manage identity, facilitate application processing, and simplify entry for travellers with legitimate identities. In this section, you will learn about biometric requirements and exemptions. For IRCC's authority to collect biometric information, please refer to the Legal references related to Biometrics and Identity Management.
5.1. What Biometrics are Collected? The following information is collected by IRCC from the applicant, at the session where biometrics are enrolled:
- biographic data: name, date of birth, and other personal details of an applicant as listed on the biographic data page of the applicant's passport or travel document
- 10 fingerprints: fingerprints of the applicant, captured electronically during the biometrics collection session, using an electronic fingerprint-capture device. Not everyone is able to give high quality fingerprints, learn more about processing poor quality fingerprints.
- photograph: a digital photograph of the applicant

5.2. Who Must Provide Biometrics? Biometric collection is mandatory for all foreign nationals, between the ages of 14 and 79 who are:
- applying for a temporary resident visa
- applying for a work permit or a study permit, (excluding U.S. nationals)
- extension of their stay in Canada
- a work or study permit extension
- applying for permanent residence
- claiming refugee or asylum status There is a processing and collection fee that must be paid each time an applicant provides their biometric information unless they are exempt from paying fees.
- All individual applicants pay CAD$85 to provide their biometrics (unless biometric fee exempt). Families applying together pay a maximum total fee of CAD$170. A maximum fee of CAD$255 applies for groups of three or more performing artists and their staff who are applying for a work permit at the same time.
- The biometric fee is non-refundable once the service has been rendered.
5.3. Which Applicants are Exempted from Submitting Biometrics? Biometrics exemptions are listed under R12.2(1)and R12.6, R12.7 and R12.8 of the IRPR. The exemption list includes but is not limited to:
- applicants younger than 14 years or older than 79 years old at the time of their application
- accredited diplomats of other countries and the United Nations, coming to Canada on official travel
- visa-exempt foreign nationals coming to Canada as visitors
- heads of state and heads of government

## 5.4. Where do Foreign Nationals Go to Provide their Biometrics?

For applicants who need to give their biometrics for a TR application, it is best to apply online or in person at a Visa Application Centre (VAC).

- Online applicants must pay the biometrics fee when they submit their application to receive their Biometrics Instruction Letter (BIL) by email within 24 hours. The letter will direct them to a list of biometrics collection service locations.
- Applicants who apply in person at a VAC do not need to wait to receive a biometrics instruction letter. They can submit their application, pay the biometrics collection fee, based on the payment method available at the VAC, and give their biometrics at the same time. Foreign nationals can go to one of these official locations to give their biometrics (fingerprints and photograph):
- outside Canada and the U.S.
- at one of Canada's VAC's worldwide clients may enrol biometrics with or without a BIL
- an office outside Canada in exceptional circumstances
- in the United States
- at one of the Application Support Centres (ASC) clients can only enrol biometrics with a BIL
- at the port of entry
- asylum claimants, and visa-exempt travellers eligible to apply for a work or study permit at the port of entry

5.5. Partial Enrolment Designated officers have the discretion to exempt applicants from providing one or both pieces of biometric information (fingerprints and photo), if it is determined that the collection of biometric information is impossible or not feasible. For more information, refer to Exemption-Impossible or Not Feasible.
5.6. What is the Validity Period of Biometrics for Temporary Residents? With the implementation of the 1 in 10 policy in the temporary residence stream, biometrics can be reused for subsequent temporary residence applications. The validity period is the period during which previously enrolled biometrics may be reused for subsequent temporary residence applications or requests. For example, if a person is applying for a TRV, a study permit, or a work permit, they only need to give their biometrics once every 10 years. They will not have to provide them again until the 10-year period expires. GCMS will automatically associate valid biometrics to a client's application if they are eligible for 1 in 10. Applicants can find out if their biometrics are still valid and when they expire by using the Check Status Tool.

# TR Decision Making

NOTE: In cases where applicants do not benefit from the 1 in 10 policy, the validity date of their biometrics will be set to the expiry date of the permit or visa counterfoil if the application is “Approved”. If the application is “Refused" or "Withdrawn", it will be set to the “Application Closed Date". A note should be entered in the system to indicate that the applicant does not qualify for the 1 in 10 policy.

# 5.7. How to Interpret Status and Results?

After the biometric enrollment has been sent to the RCMP, they will return a search result that will advise the officer if the RCMP already has those fingerprints on file in one of three biometric databases. The RCMP checks the fingerprints against their national repository of criminal records, the immigration database and also the legacy refugee claimant database. The status of the sub-activity in GCMS will tell you if the fingerprints were known to the RCMP and also if they were of sufficient quality to complete a search.

The most common statuses are:

- “Received – No reportable trace (NRT)": the applicant's fingerprints do not match any existing record in the RCMP criminal or immigration databases. There are no admissibility or identity concerns based on the client's fingerprints. •“Received – IMM": the applicant's fingerprints were submitted previously as part of an immigration application. The RCMP will return the biographic details associated with those fingerprints from their database. If their information is different than the information on file in GCMS the officer should review the records and follow up, as needed.
- “Received – CPIC": the applicant's fingerprints are in the national repository of criminal records. The officer must wait for the Biometric Assessment Unit (BAU) to assess the information the RCMP has on file, enter their opinion in GCMS, and update the officer. The officer may also wish to review the previous record and follow up, as needed.
- “Poor quality": the RCMP cannot conduct a search against their databases as the quality of the fingerprints provided was poor. Learn more about processing poor quality fingerprints.

# Unit 2: Visitor Applications

### About this Unit

In this unit, you will learn how to process TR applications under the visitor class. Foreign nationals from around the globe visit Canada every year. Some require a TRV or an eTA to travel to Canada, while others may be exempt.

In this unit of the eWorkbook and during the virtual session, you will practice assessing applications and making decisions using scenarios and case studies. Although fictitious, the scenarios represent common situations you will encounter as an officer.

Although some content in your eWorkbook applies to specific networks, it will be useful for you to learn about them as there are linkages between your work and those of your colleagues in other networks. For example, TRV applications are processed by officers outside Canada or officers at the Case Processing Center – Ottawa (CPC-O). Electronic travel authorization applications are mainly

## Why?

Most of TR applications are visitor applications. Depending in which team you work on, it may be quite likely that the majority of TR applications you will process will be under the visitor class. Additionally, there are a number of similarities between visitor and two other classes of temporary residence: international students and temporary foreign workers. Developing skills to assess visitor applications will also help you in processing international student and temporary foreign worker applications.

### How?

You will be building on your prior learning from the e-Introduction to Immigration (CC8200) and Introduction to Decision Making (CC8307). You will complete this workbook content and exercises. Then, you will join the group learning session as per the established schedule. The unit contains:

Completion of this unit should take approximately four hours. We recommend you take a short break every 50-60 minutes, refresh, and return to complete the remaining sections.

## TR Decision Making

Introduction

To begin, do you know who is considered to be a foreign national? A2(1) states: a foreign national is a person who is not a Canadian citizen or a permanent resident, and includes a stateless person.

A Canadian citizen means a citizen referred to in subsection 3(1) of the Citizenship Act and a permanent resident means a person who has acquired permanent resident status and has not subsequently lost that status under section 46 of IRPA These persons, and every person registered as an Indian under the ndían Act do not need a temporary resident visa to come to Canada as they have a right to enter as per subsections 19(1) and 19(2) of IRPA.

As you have learned in e-Introduction to Immigration, there are several reasons why a foreign national comes to Canada. Some of these reasons may be:

- tourism, visiting family or friends
- study
- work temporarily
In this unit, we will focus on foreign nationals wanting to come to Canada as a temporary resident, and more specifically as a visitor.

Do you know what a “temporary resident" is?

A “temporary resident" is a foreign national who is legally authorized to enter Canada for a temporary purpose. They hold temporary resident status when they have been found to meet the requirements of the legislation to enter and/or remain in Canada as a visitor, student, worker or temporary resident permit holder. Only foreign nationals physically in Canada hold temporary resident status.

Please take a few minutes to review the legislative references for visitors that you will explore throughout the unit.

## Decision Making – Key Steps when Assessing Visitor Applications

International Network-Use these five key steps to help you get started with your decision making process when assessing a temporary resident visa application. As we expand on each step, they will also guide you through the learning points of the unit.

STEP 1: Determine if they are a foreign national If a foreign national, proceed to STEP 2.If Canadian Citizen, refer to A19(1) If permanent resident, refer to procedures re. PRTDs.

# STEP 2: Determine if a TRV or an ETA is required [A11(1), R7(1), R7.1(1)]

If a TRV is required, proceed to STEP 3. If TRV exempt, does the foreign national require an eTA? If yes, eTA application online (refer to the section of the eWorkbook covering eTAs). STEP 3: Determine if the foreign national will leave by the end of the period authorized for their stay [R179(b)], holds a valid travel document [R179(c)], and meets the requirements of R30 if they must submit to a medical examination [R179(f)] If satisfied, proceed to STEP 4. If not satisfied, refuse the TRV application. ## TR Decision Making

1. Temporary Resident Visa & Electronic Travel Authorization

In the e-Introduction to Immigration (CC8200), you learned that the first step is to apply for a visa or for any other document required by the regulations as per A11(1) of the IRPA. A foreign national who seeks to enter or remain in Canada must have the visa or other documents required under the regulations and show that they will leave Canada by the end of their period of authorized stay A20(1)(b). Application before entering Canada A11(1) states “A foreign national must, before entering Canada, apply to an officer for a visa or for any other document required by the regulations. The visa or document may be issued if, following an examination, the officer is satisfied that the foreign national is not inadmissible and meets the requirements of this Act." Documents Required Before Entry R7(1) states “A foreign national may not enter Canada to remain on a temporary basis without first obtaining a temporary resident visa."
## Obligation on entry

A20(1)(b) states “Every foreign national, other than a foreign national referred to in section 19, who seeks to enter or remain in Canada must establish to become a temporary resident, that they hold the visa or other document required under regulations and will leave Canada by the end of the period authorized for their stay."

You also learned that if a foreign national does not require a TRV as perR7(2), which refers to R190, they may require an eTA as per R7.1(1), unless exempt from this requirement. Note: A foreign national cannot hold a TRV and an eTA. It is either one or the other, unless exempt.

Before continuing, let's take a few minutes to test your current knowledge about the TRV and the eTA requirement. This activity will set the platform to building a stronger foundation for you to make decisions on visitor applications.

2.2.3 Dual Intent

IRPA includes a section about foreign nationals who have dual intent, which means one for temporary residence and one for permanent residence. A22(2) of IRPA addresses this situation by stating the following: “An intention by a foreign national to become a permanent resident does not preclude them from becoming a temporary resident if the officer is satisfied that they will leave Canada by the end of the period authorized for their stay."
|44 A-2021-22877-000586

migration, Refugees Immigration, Réfugié and Citizenship Canadaet Citoyenneté Cana Iformat nt L'information divulguée en vertu de la [oi sur l’accès à Finfo

## TR Decision Making

Dual intent is present when a foreign national who has applied or may apply for permanent residence also applies to enter Canada temporarily as a visitor, student or worker. IRPA recognizes that a person may have “dual intent" of immigrating (if permitted to do so) and of abiding by the conditions of temporary entry. Therefore, to qualify for a TRV in cases where there is dual intent, foreign nationals must satisfy you that they can and will leave Canada at the end of the authorized period of stay if their application for permanent residence is not finalized or is refused. A22(2 reiterates the essential obligation of a TR. In some cases, TRs may never leave Canada because they can become permanent residents without having to leave. There is nothing wrong with this. However, if their TR status were to end or if they were ordered to leave, they must leave Canada even if they have a PR application in progress. To meet the requirements, they must have a genuine intent to enter Canada temporarily in the short term, even if they have a genuine long-term intent to remain permanently.

## Example of dual intent:

The wish to await the outcome of a PR application in Canada may have legitimate reasons, i.e. a family class applicant may have little to return to in their country and therefore prefers to remain close to family members in Canada. Students or temporary workers may not wish to disrupt their studies/employment to return to their homeland while awaiting the outcome of their application for permanent residence.

Note: You are not obliged to extend TR status if there is a PR application in progress. Evaluate the factors to approve or refuse the

request for a TR extension.

For more information, refer to Temporary Residents: Dual Intent.

The passport must be valid for the duration of their stay. Therefore, you cannot issue a visa or extend status beyond the validity of passport or the travel document.

## TR Decision Making

The Act does not differentiate between types of evidence and does not impose any formal rules on admissibility. There are different types of evidence as seen in Unit 3 of the Introduction to Decision Making course.

5.1. Evidence to Support a Temporary Resident Visa or an Extension of Stay as a Visitor

An assessment of the evidence will assess its relevance and reliability and then determine if the evidence is sufficient to establish that the foreign national meets the requirements to be issued a TRV or a Visitor record following an application. Do you need to consider all of the evidence available? Yes!

## TR Decision Making

Once you have identified the evidence, assess its relevance and reliability and then determine if the evidence is sufficient to establish that the foreign national meets the requirements to be issued a TRV or a visitor record following an application.

### Example:

1) A visitor submits a letter from a friend stating that the foreign national is a good person: this is irrelevant as the requirements are not about the personality of the foreign national. Therefore, you would not have to mention this letter.
2) A visitor submits a letter from parents stating they will support their son financially while in Canada. You conclude that the foreign national does not have sufficient funds. You must address this letter because it is material to your conclusion and explain why this letter did not satisfy you.
You will assign weight to the evidence, by assessing them individually, based on the reliability of the source or its content, and by comparison to the entirety of the evidence.Let's look at an example for a temporary resident:

# Example:

A visitor requesting a visitor record extension is submitting proof of funds to demonstrate that they can sustain themselves for the duration of their requested period of stay. On one hand, you may give little weight to a letter from a parent, because the parent has an interest in the outcome of the application. However, if the content of the parent's letter is confirmed with a Notice of Assessment and a letter from the parent's employer, then you would give it more weight.

NOTE: Whenever the applicant's credibility is in question, or there is concern that a document that is submitted is altered or fraudulent, it is imperative that a procedural fairness exchange occur either by a Procedural Fairness Letter or an interview. The designated officer must consider the applicant's responses and determine whether the basis for refusal stands. It is important to know that credibility has to do with the veracity, usually of the person, but could be applied to a document. Reliability is maybe closer to accuracy, neutrality etc. Therefore you could have a credible applicant that provides information that is not reliable. The term credibility is best used where one would not believe something because it is possibly a lie, fraud or misrepresentation.

It is not generally necessary to proceed with procedural fairness for information that is unreliable, but it is (with rare exception) necessary to proceed with procedural fairness if there are credibility concerns.

9.5. Inadmissibility As seen earlier, to extend temporary resident status to a foreign national, they must not be inadmissible. NOTE: If the application has passed eligibility and results from partner agencies have raised admissibility concerns under A34, A35 or A37, stage 2 decision makers are to transfer the application to the Domestic Network's Centre of Expertise in Security Cases for assessment. This procedure only applies to applications submitted in Canada where the applicant or dependant of concern is in Canada. Certain foreign nationals in Canada that are under Visitor status are authorized to study and work in Canada without a study or work permit. These foreign nationals are not considered to be inadmissible if they meet the requirement of studying or working without a permit. You will learn more about these types of foreign nationals in Unit 3 International Student Applications and Unit 4 Temporary Worker Applications.
10. Make a Decision – Extensions R181(2) provides for officers to consider requests for extensions of temporary resident status and to vary conditions of entry. It states that if, following examination, it is established that the foreign national continues to meet the criteria outlined in R179, that an officer shall extend that status. It does not however, set out any specific criteria for granting or refusing an application to extend temporary resident status or to vary or cancel conditions of entry. As a general rule, therefore, the statutory criteria governing admissibility (A34-A42) and the criteria in R179will apply to decisions respecting these two issues. The decision to extend or refuse an application will often require an assessment of positive factors, i.e. those that support an extension and negative factors, i.e. those that support a refusal. It is your responsibility to weigh all factors and to make, on balance, a decision based on the various considerations. Earlier in this unit, you saw what types of evidence could be provided with a visitor application. If a foreign national wishes to extend their stay in Canada, would the evidence be the same or would they be different? A foreign national would need to satisfy you of the reasons why they want to extend their stay. What have they been doing in Canada? Do they have any evidence of what they have been doing? Have their circumstances changed? What are their ties with their home country? Does the foreign national still have a job in their country? Has the foreign national provided evidence that their leave has been extended? Does the foreign national have sufficient funds to support themselves according to the reasons of extension?

10.1. Reject Visitor Extension If the paper application request for extending temporary resident status is incomplete for missing fees or signature, the case processing center returns the application to the foreign national. The application is considered to have never been received, no maintained status is granted, and the foreign national will be considered in status until the original TR document expires.
10.2. Visitor Extension Referral In certain situations, applications may need to be referred because of program integrity issues or in situations where there is a potential refusal based on criminality, security or medical inadmissibility, which could lead to an A44 report and admissibility hearing.
10.3. Visitor Extension Approval If you have determined that the foreign national meets the eligibility and admissibility requirements, approve the visitor extension application.
10.4. Visitor Extension Refusal If you have determined that the foreign national does not meet either the eligibility or admissibility requirements, refuse the TRV application. If the foreign national is still in status, you should:
- remind the foreign national of the expiry date of their current status or document
- explain the consequences of overstaying past that expiry date

# Unit 3: International Student Applications

About this Unit In this unit, you will learn about temporary residents who want to come to Canada, or are in Canada, to study. Foreign students are persons who may obtain TR status and who:

- have been issued study permits, or are authorized by the Regulations (R) to study without study permits.
Foreign students are a valuable part of our Immigration Program. One of the objectives of the IRPA is to facilitate the entry of visitors, students and temporary workers for purposes such as trade, commerce, tourism, international understanding and cultural, educational and scientific activities. Foreign students benefit Canada by bringing cultural enrichment to the Canadian education scene and by helping to diversify the economy and boost the educational system.

#### TR Decision Making

To determine if a foreign national meets the requirements, you will need to assess the evidence presented by the foreign national. In order to do so, you will:

- learn in detail the requirements to study in Canada
- explore the type of evidence required to meet eligibility and admissibility criteria
- practice assessing and making decisions through exercise scenarios
## Objective

At the end of this unit, you will be able to process applications for authorization to study in Canada consistent with the Immigration Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the Immigration Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) and the relevant program delivery instructions (PDI).

### Outline

You will explore information and complete exercises on the following:

- determining if an activity is considered studies
- determining if a study permit is required
- taking a closer look at the designated learning institution
- eligibility and admissibility to be issued a study permit
- making the final decision
# Why?

Studying the material in this eWorkbook will help you to explore and navigate through the policies and legal requirements for international students. Additionally, there are a number of similarities between the other classes of temporary residence; therefore, developing skills to assess student applications will also help you in processing visitor and worker applications.

Introduction

As you saw in the Unit 2 Visitor Applications, A11(1) states that a foreign national must apply for a visa or other document required by the Regulations before entering Canada. 4.1.3 Financial Resources A foreign student wanting to study in Canada must prove that they have sufficient funds to support themselves without working in Canada, as per R220.
### This includes:

- paying their yearly tuition
- maintaining themselves and their accompanying family members during their proposed stay in Canada
- being able to pay the transportation costs to and from Canada
Students are required to demonstrate financial sufficiency for only the first year of studies, regardless of the duration of the course or program of studies in which they are enrolled. In other words, a single student entering a four-year degree program with an annual tuition fee of $15,000 must demonstrate funds of $15,000 to satisfy the requirements, and not the full $60,000 which would be required for four years. Officers should be satisfied, however, that the probability of funding for future years does exist i.e., parents are employed, scholarship is for more than one year.

In assessing the adequacy of a student's financial resources, officers may exercise discretion in the documentation they request from applicants. In situations where student applicants generally pose a very low risk regarding funds, officers may choose to limit or

# waive routine requirements for documentary evidence.

For more information, refer to Study permits: Assessing the application, specifically the section on financial sufficiency. Use it as a guideline when assessing financial viability.

4.1.4 Certificat d’acceptation du Québec

A Certificat d’acceptation du Québec (CAQ) is an authorization from the Government of Quebec that authorizes someone to study in that province. You shall not issue a study permit to a foreign national who intends to study in the province of Quebec if the laws require that the foreign national holds a CAQ R216(3).

With few exemptions, all Quebec-bound foreign nationals must submit a CAQ or a confirmation letter from the Ministère de l’Immigration, de la Francisation et de l’Intégration (MIFl) when applying for a study permit. NOTE: A confirmation letter from MIFI is equivalent to the CAQ.

For more information about special considerations and CAQ exemptions for students destined to Quebec, refer to_Study permits: Students destined to Quebec.

4.1.5 Passport

Foreign students must meet the passport requirements outlined in R52(1).

A foreign national who wishes to extend their student status in Canada must hold a passport or travel document that is valid for the length of their proposed stay. A foreign national is not required to have a passport valid for the entire duration of their course of studies, but the validity of the permit cannot go beyond the passport expiry date R179(c), R181(2) and R183(2)(c).

4.1.6 Custodianship

Every unaccompanied minor child (less than 17 years of age at the time of application) in Canada on study permit needs a custodian.

All minor applicants for study permit extensions must supply a notarized declaration, one signed by the parents or legal guardians in the country of origin and one signed by the custodian in Canada, stating that arrangements have been made for the custodian to act in place of a parent. You have to be satisfied that adequate arrangements are in place.

Custodians should be 19 years of age or older, regardless of the province of destination.

4.2. Are the Requirements for the Issuance of a Study Permit Met? It is important to ensure that the requirements for the issuance of a study permit are met. R216(1) outlines when an officer shall issue a study permit; i.e. if, following an examination, it is established that:
(a) the foreign national applied for the study permit properly
(b) the foreign national will leave Canada by the end of the period authorized for their stay
(c) the foreign national meets the requirements
(d) the foreign national meets the medical requirements R30(2) and (3)
(e) the foreign national has been accepted to undertake a program of study at a designated learning institution
R217(2) – outlines that an officer shall only renew the study permit if foreign national continues to meet the requirements of R216, the specific requirements of a student.

4.2.1 Admissibility Requirements As you have learned in Unit 2 Visitor Applications, you need to be satisfied that the applicants are not inadmissible (A34 to A42).

## TR Decision Making

As stated in A11(1) 'A foreign national must, before entering Canada, apply to an officer for a visa or for any other document required by the regulations. The visa or document may be issued if, following an examination, the officer is satisfied that the foreign national is not inadmissible and meets the requirements of this Act'.

4.2.2 Six-month Ban Provision R221 states that a study permit shall not be issued to a foreign national who has engaged in unauthorized work or study in Canada or who has failed to comply with a condition of a permit unless:
(a) a period of six months has elapsed since the cessation of the unauthorized work or study or failure to comply with a condition
(b) the work or study was unauthorized by reason only that the foreign national did not comply with conditions imposed under paragraph 185(a), any of subparagraphs 185(b)(i) to (iii) or paragraph 185(c); or
(c) the foreign national was subsequently issued a temporary resident permit under subsection 24(1) of the Act
When the officer reviews an application, they will first check GCMS to determine if there is anything that would prevent the foreign national from entering. They will verify the status of the foreign national in reviewing case notes. Generally you need to determine whether the "six-month ban" on the issuance of a study permit applies.

The lapse of six months would not apply in the case of inland applications because the foreign national would first have to get their status restored prior to being issued a study permit (refer to Restoration R182).

4.3. Referral In certain situations, applications may need to be referred because of program integrity issues or in situations where there is a potential refusal based on criminality, security or medical inadmissibility, which could lead to an A44 report and admissibility hearing. Referral criteria does change frequently so refer to Program Delivery Updates regularly for any changes.
4.4. Assess the Evidence We just covered the eligibility requirements for a study permit. Foreign nationals will need to satisfy you they meet those requirements.

5. Make the Final Decision At this stage, you should have made your decision to approve, refuse or refer. Once your decision is made, you have to document your decision, generate the appropriate documents and inform the applicant.
5.1. Approve If you have determined that the foreign national meets the eligibility requirements and is not inadmissible, approve the study permit application. For more information on processing steps, refer to Study permits: Final decisions.
# 5.2. Refuse

If you have determined that the foreign national does not meet either the eligibility requirements or is inadmissible, refuse the study permit application. Remember that in some cases, a procedural fairness letter should be sent and opportunity to respond given before a final decision can be made.

For more information on procedural fairness, refer toProcedural fairness. For more information on processing steps, refer to Study permits: Final decisions.

5.3. Validity Periods Once you have determined that a student meets the requirements, you should eliminate or at least minimize further transactions with the student. One of the most effective ways to minimize further transactions is to issue long-term study permits. As per R222(1), the validity of a study permit corresponds to the length of the program of studies plus 90 days following program completion, therefore, a study permit becomes invalid 90 days after the day the student completes their course or program of study.

## Key Points to Remember

- as per R9(1), all foreign nationals are required to obtain a study permit for engaging in academic, professional, vocational or other education or training that is more than six months in duration at a DL in Canada, unless exempted a foreign national is exempt from a study permit requirement if they are described as being authorized to study without the issuance of a study permit in R188 or A30(2)
- a foreign national can apply for a study permit before entry, on entry or after entry (R213, R214 and R215)
- to be eligible for a study permit, a foreign national needs to meet the general requirements for all temporary residents R179 as well as the specific requirements of R216 or R217

# TR Decision Making

In some cases, you may need to conduct an interview with the foreign national in person or by phone. In certain situations, you may need to use the services of an interpreter. Remember that the interpreter cannot be a friend or family member of the foreign national. They must be an accredited interpreter. It should also be noted that counsel and representatives cannot act as interpreters.

When IRCC is providing an interpreter and is paying for the interpretation services offered to the clients, the department uses the interpreters from the Immigration Refugee Board of Canada (IRB) list of accredited and security-cleared interpreters. Interpretation services at Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) are guided by the Standard Interpretation Service Contractor Clauses and Conditions.

For guidelines to conduct an interview and using the services of an interpreter, see Interviews and Interpreters. For guidelines on the role of a representatives, see Use of Representatives: Counselling Applicants During Interview

Procedural Fairness Decision makers must follow the rules of procedural fairness throughout the decision-making process. Procedural fairness requires that foreign nationals:

- are provided with a fair and unbiased assessment of their application are informed of the decision maker's concerns have a meaningful opportunity to provide a response to concerns about their application For more information refer to Procedural fairness.

TR Decision Making

General Steps for Assessing a Study Permit Application You should check to ensure that all documents are enclosed with the application package and these have been properly completed. You should also:

- ensure that the application form has been properly completed and signed by the applicant
- determine whether a fee is required and that payment has been included
- for initial and new study permit applications, review Study permits: Letter of acceptance to make sure that it is issued by a DLI and that it covers all the basic necessary information
- for study permit applications to extend status in Canada, review the letter of enrolment or transcript, or the letter issued by the DLl to ensure that the student is in compliance with their study permit decisions (e.g., enrolled and actively pursuing studies).
Refer to Study permits: Final decisions for more information

- review the financial documents to determine if adequate financial resources are available to support the applicant and any accompanying family members for the first year of the course of study. Applications for extensions must meet the same requirement.
Refer to financial sufficiency under Study permits: Assessing the application for more information

- verify that the applicant has a valid passport or travel document
- verify that the applicant has a valid CAQ, if they are destined to a designated learning institution in Quebec

# IRPA/IRPRDescription

States that an officer shall issue a temporary resident visa to a foreign national if, following an examination, it is established that the foreign national:

a) applied for a temporary resident visa as a member of the visitor, worker or student class;
b) will leave Canada by the end of the period authorized for their stay;
## R179

c) holds a valid passport or travel document;
d) meets the class requirements;
e) is not inadmissible; and
f) meets the medical requirements.
Outlines when an officer shall issue a work permit; i.e. if, following an examination, it is established that:

a)the foreign national applied for the work permit properly;
b) the foreign national will leave Canada at the end of the period authorized for their stay;
c)the foreign national;
i. is described in section 206 or 208; ii. intends to perform work described in section 204 or 205 but does not have a job offer; ii.1 intends to perform work described in section 204or 205 and has a job offer determined to be:
## R200(1) A. genuine,

B. during the preceding six years,
I. job offer – same occupation, wages and working hours are substantially the same, II. if not, is able to justify changes,
iii. has been offered employment and an ESDC confirmation has been received confirming that the offer is genuine and there will be a neutral or positive benefit to the Canadian economy,

d)[Repealed, SOR/2004-167, s. 56];
e) medical requirements in section 30(2) and (3) are met.
R200(1)(b) does not apply to a foreign national who satisfies the criteria in R206 or R207(c) or (d).

# IRPA/IRPR Description

An officer shall not issue a work permit to a foreign national if:

(a) there are grounds to believe the foreign national cannot perform the work,

Ch_01_04_01_A_01 EXERCISE: What Documents are Acceptable for Entering Canada? - Answers As per R52(1), a foreign national seeking to become a temporary resident must hold one of the following documents that is valid for the period authorized for their stay:

(a) a passport that was issued by the country of which the foreign national is a citizen or national, that does not prohibit travel to Canada and that the foreign national may use to enter the country of issue;
(b) a travel document that was issued by the country of which the foreign national is a citizen or national, that does not prohibit travel to Canada and that the foreign national may use to enter the country of issue;
(c) an identity or travel document that was issued by a country, that does not prohibit travel to Canada, that the foreign national may use to enter the country of issue and that is of the type issued by that country to non-national residents, refugees or stateless persons who are unable to obtain a passport or other travel document from their country of citizenship or nationality or who have no country of citizenship or nationality;
(d) a laissez-passer that was issued by the United Nations;
(e) a passport or travel document that was issued by the Palestinian Authority;
(f) a document that was issued by the Organization of American States and is entitled “Official Travel Document";
(g) a passport issued by the United Kingdom to a British Overseas Citizen;
(h) a passport issued by the United Kingdom to a British National (Overseas), as a person born, naturalized or registered in Hong Kong;
(i) a passport issued by the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China; or
(j) a passport issued by the United Kingdom to a British Subject.

Ch_01_04_02_A_01 EXERCISE: Who is Exempt from Having a Valid Travel Document to Enter Canada as a TR? - Answers

As per R52(2), the following foreign nationals are exempt from the requirement of passports, travel document or identity documents:

(a) citizens of the United States;
(b) persons seeking to enter Canada from the United States or St. Pierre and Miquelon who have been lawfully admitted to the United States for permanent residence;
(c) residents of Greenland seeking to enter Canada from Greenland;
(d) persons seeking to enter Canada from St. Pierre and Miquelon who are citizens of France and residents of St. Pierre and Miquelon;
(e) members of the armed forces of a country that is a designated state for the purposes of the Visiting Forces Act who are seeking entry in order to carry out official duties, other than persons who have been designated as a civilian component of those armed forces;
(f) persons who are seeking to enter Canada as, or in order to become, members of a crew of a means of air transportation and who hold an airline flight crew licence or crew member certificate issued in accordance with International Civil Aviation Organization specifications; or
(g) persons seeking to enter Canada as members of a crew who hold a seafarer's identity document issued under International Labour Organization conventions and are members of the crew of the vessel that carries them to Canada.

# TR Decision Making

CH_01_05_05_A_01 EXERCISE: Biometrics – Answers

1. An applicant, that turned 14 years old after her application was submitted, is required to provide biometrics. True or False? This is false because the biometric requirement is based on the age the applicant at the time of application.
2. The RCMP returns the response Received – CPIC in response to Tina's biometric enrollment. A match for her fingerprints has been found in the immigration database. True or False? "Received – CPIC” means that the applicant's fingerprints are in the national repository of criminal records. Therefore, this is false. Received – IMM means that the applicant's fingerprints were submitted previously to the RCMP as part of an immigration application.
3. Harpreet is applying for a study permit and needs to submit biometrics as he has never applied to come to Canada before. True or False? True. As of December 31, 2018, nationals of India are required to provide their biometrics in support of a TR, PR, and REF-CLM. Should nationals of India have an outstanding application submitted before December 31st 2018, they are biometrically exempt. The exemption is based on the date IRCC's received the application (i.e. Rec'd Date).
4. Even though Juan has provided his biometrics within the last 10 years for a previous TR application, he is required to submit new biometrics for his new TR application. True or False? With the implementation of the 1 in 10 policy in the temporary residence stream, biometrics can be re-used for subsequent temporary residence applications. This is false because the applicant provided his biometrics within the last ten years, therefore his biometrics can be used for his subsequent TR application as it is still valid.

5. Designated officers have the discretion to exempt applications from providing one or both pieces of biometric information.
### True or False?

This is true. Designated officers have the discretion to exempt applicants from providing one or both pieces of biometric information (fingerprints and photo), if it is determined that the collection of biometric information is impossible or not feasible.
