# Unit 2: Visitor Applications

CH_02_01_00_A_01 REVIEW YOUR CURRENT KNOWLEDGE: TRV or eTA-Answers

1. The foreign nationals should submit their application either online or to the office outside Canada that is responsible for serving the country in which they have been lawfully admitted or their country of nationality. For more information, refer to the list of countries and corresponding offices.
2. Paragraph 7(2) of IRPA states the foreign nationals who are exempted from obtaining a temporary resident visa. R7(2)(a) states that a temporary resident visa requirement does not apply to a foreign national who is exempted under Division 5 of Part 9 of the regulations. This refers directly to R190(1), R190(2), R190(2.1), R190(3), R190(3.1) which identify the foreign nationals that are exempt from the requirement to obtain a TRV. •R190(1)identifies those that are exempt based on nationality •R190(2)identifies those that are exempt based on documents
- R190(3) identifies those that are exempt based on purpose of entry
3. Yes. Foreign nationals that are visa-exempt are required to obtain an eTA before travelling to Canada by air, unless otherwise exempted from the requirement.
4. No, there are foreign nationals that are exempt from both a TRV and an eTA such as US citizens and foreign nationals travelling in or transiting through Canada by land, sea, or rail. For more information, refer to R7.1(2), (3). These paragraphs describe the foreign nationals who are exempt from the eTA requirement.

5. Foreign nationals need to apply online using the Come to Canada Wizard. The eTA is an automated process if there are no concerns. If there are concerns (ex. criminality), the eTA will drop out of the automated process and will go for review with an officer at OSC or to an office outside Canada if local information is required.
6. An eTA is valid for five years or until foreign national's passport expires, whichever comes first. An eTA can also be cancelled by a designated officer. Once cancelled, the eTA is no longer valid.

7. eTA applications fall out of the automated process and are referred to an officer for the following reasons:
- Identity reconciliation
- Derogatory information
- eTA application hits against the Lost, Stolen and Fraudulent Document Database
- Canadian citizen or permanent resident
- Adverse information on file

For more information, refer to manually processing electronic travel authorization applications section.

CH_02_02_00_A_01 EXERCISE: Raj's Story-Answer A foreign national who wants to come to Canada must meet the general requirements as per R179. The general requirements for a temporary resident are:

(a) has applied in accordance with these Regulations for a temporary resident visa as a member of the visitor, worker or student class;
(b) will leave Canada by the end of the period authorized for their stay under Division 2;
(c) holds a passport or other document that they may use to enter the country that issued it or another country;
(d) meets the requirements applicable to that class;
(e) is not inadmissible;
(f) meets the requirements of subsections 30(2) and (3), if they must submit to a medical examination under paragraph 16(2)(b) of the Act; and
(g) is not the subject of a declaration made under subsection 22.1(1) of the Act. 6Return

# TR Decision Making

WhatQuestions_Consider_A EXERCISE: What Questions Would You Consider-Answers There are several factors to consider when assessing a TRV or a request to extend a TR stay. The following is a list of questions you could ask yourself to determine if the foreign national will leave at the end of their authorized stay.

Purpose of trip: What will they be doing in Canada? Amount of time requested What is the duration of the visit? Is it reasonable in relation to their situation?

What will the person be doing in Canada? Does the proposed trip to Canada make sense? What have they done while in Canada? Activities while in Canada Have they had previous overstays?

i.e. criminality, employment, refugee claim, touring, visiting relatives, etc. Are the plans well thought, considering their circumstances back in their home country?
Reason(s) for the request i.e. One more month to see snow might be reasonable but is six months? Did the foreign national already experience winter in Canada? Amount of time already in As above, it is reasonable? Has the time spent in Canada sufficient to fulfill their purpose for Canada coming to Canada? Ties to their country of residence: Are the foreign national's ties to their country of residence sufficiently strong to ensure they will leave Canada at the end of the authorized stay? Location of dependants Is the whole family in Canada or are there spouse/children to go back to in their home country?

## TR Decision Making

EXERCISE: Authorized Period of Stay-Answers R183(4) - The period authorized for a temporary resident's stay ends on the earliest of

(a) the day on which the temporary resident leaves Canada without obtaining prior authorization to re-enter Canada;
(b) the day on which their permit becomes invalid, in the case of a temporary resident who has been issued either a work permit or a study permit;
(c) the day on which any temporary resident permit issued to the temporary resident is no longer valid under section 63;
(d) the day on which the period authorized under subsection (2) ends, if paragraphs (a) to (c) do not apply.
R183(5) – If a TR has applied for an extension of the period of authorized stay and a decision is not made on the application by the end of the period authorized for their stay, the period is extended until

(a) the day on which a decision is made, if the application is refused; or
(b) the end of the new period authorized for their stay, if the application is allowed.

Answer 5:

1) Reasonable grounds to believe: If there are reasonable grounds to believe that a foreign national may be inadmissible under A38(1), an officer may request a medical examination. (i.e. information in the file shows they may have a mental illness that might be a danger to the safety). Reasonable grounds to believe means that the officer has more than a mere suspicion. The officer must have more facts to be able to conclude that there are reasonable grounds to believe.
2) Persons who are applying for a Super visa
## 3) Some temporary residents seeking medical treatment in Canada

Answer 6: If a foreign national plans to visit Canada for six months or less, a medical examination is not required unless the foreign national intends to work in an occupation in which the protection of public health is essential and you don't have reasonable grounds to believe that the foreign national may be medically inadmissible.

Answer 7: As per R30(1)(a)(ii), foreign nationals seeking to come to Canada for more than six months require a medical examination if they have resided in a designated country for six consecutive months or more within the year preceding the date of their application (what we call the 6 + 6 Rule). NOTE: The designated country is the country where the foreign national has resided six months or more. It is not necessarily where they are nationals. Medical examination is also required for:

- Foreign nationals who are seeking to work in occupations in which the protection of public health is essential, regardless of the length of stay
- Foreign nationals who you have reasonable grounds to believe are inadmissible under A38(1), as per R30(1)(a)(iv), regardless of the length of stay

REVIEW YOUR CURRENT KNOWLEDGE: Status—Answers Answer 1:

There are three ways that a temporary resident can lose their status in Canada as per A47.

As you have learned in the e-Introduction to Immigration, a foreign national loses temporary resident status at per A47:

(a) At the end of the period for which they are authorized to remain in Canada;
(b) On a determination by an officer or the Immigration Division that they have failed to comply with any other requirement of this Act; or
(c) On cancellation of their temporary resident permit.
If a foreign national is not in status, then they are in violation of A29(2) and are therefore inadmissible under A41(a)—non- compliance. A temporary resident is responsible for leaving Canada by the end of the period authorized for their stay.

## Answer 2:

The three different ways that a decision can be communicated to the foreign national when entering Canada are:

1) By verbal authorization
2) By stamping the passport
3) By issuing a Visitor Record
If there is no stamp in the passport and the foreign national has not been issued a Visitor record, the entry date can be verified by doing a query using the Entry/Exit tab in GCMS. When entering Canada, the passports are scanned electronically (PIK Process).

For more information, refer to Automated ports of entry.

Answer 1: The eligibility requirements for restoration are:

- apply within 90 days of having lost their status meet the initial requirements for their stay remain in Canada until a decision is made
- have not failed to comply with any condition imposed automatically by regulation [R183] or by an officer [R185], other than those stated below
- have lost their status only because they have failed to comply with any of the following conditions imposed by an officer: the period authorized for their stay—R185(a) o the work that they are permitted to engage in, or are prohibited from engaging in, in Canada—R185(b)(i) to (ili),
including the type of work, employer and location of work 0the studies that they are permitted to engage in, or are prohibited from engaging in, in Canada—R185(c), including the type of studies, educational institution, location or times and periods of the studies

- continue to meet the requirements of a temporary resident and the requirements of the work or study permit, as applicable
Answer 2: A foreign national who has applied to restore their status has lost their status and may not continue to work or study until their status has been restored and a new work permit or study permit has been issued.

Answer 3: No. If a foreign national leaves Canada during the process of their application to restore their status, the officer must refuse the application as they are no longer eligible to apply for restoration.

## TR Decision Making

REVIEW YOUR CURRENT KNOWLEDGE: Conditions on Temporary Residents—Answers Answer 1: R183 are the general conditions for all temporary residents, no matter if they are issued a document or not.

Answer 2:

## General Conditions—R183

The following conditions are imposed on all temporary residents

"to leave Canada by the end of the period authorized for their stay" This is one condition that is always imposed whether it is written out on a TR document or not. You should specify to each temporary resident the length of time they are permitted to remain in Canada. If you fail to specify this restriction either verbally or in writing, a time limit is still imposed. R183(1)a) From this it can be seen that if someone is admitted for more than six months, a temporary resident document must be issued. If an examining officer has any apprehension that the foreign national may not leave Canada within the time they specify, then they should document the person's file even if the period is less than six months.

"to not work, unless authorized by this Part or Part 11"

Imposing this condition may serve to discourage a visitor from working illegally; in cases where the officer is apprehensive about the person's true intentions. Also, this condition would serve to strengthen the R183(1)b) department's case against a person who is discovered working in Canada—there will be no arguments about whether or not the prohibition against working had been expressed at the time of documentation.

# Preface

Welcome to Temporary Resident Decision Making exercise booklet! Practice activities are an important part of the TR Decision Making course. This booklet will help you to apply what you have learned in the eWorkbook through practice. Here, you will find quests and exercises from the eWorkbook together with some reflective activities. Use the exercise booklet to:

- write down your answers for exercises
- reflect on your learning
- take notes and write down your questions
How to Complete the Exercise Booklet We recommend keeping your exercise booklet open at the same time as you learn with the eWorkbook. When you see a reference to an exercise in the eWorkbook, go to the same exercise in the exercise booklet and write down your answers. Check your answers with the answer keys in the eWorkbook. Please complete all practice activities to be better prepared for the virtual or classroom sessions. Remember: If you need more information, you can always email your instructor or ask a question at a virtual or classroom session. Navigation For the most part, navigating through exercise booklet is similar to any other electronic document. Just like the eWorkbook, this booklet includes external and internal hyperlinks.

## TR Decision Making

# Preface

Welcome to the Temporary Resident Decision Making course!

Prerequisites To successfully complete this eWorkbook, you must have completed: Introduction to Decision Making (CC8307) e-Introduction to Immigration (CC8200) Inadmissibility in IRPA (CC7700) Getting Ready to Learn in a Virtual Classroom (CC6520)

We are delighted to welcome you to your core training to become an effective officer assessing temporary resident (TR) applications. In this course, you will build on what you learned earlier in Introduction to Decision Making, e-Introduction to Immigration, and Inadmissibility in IRPA. You will get to practice making decisions and delve deeper into the TR requirements through case studies and exercises.

A group of subject matter experts, including representatives from the International (IN), Domestic (DN) and Centralized (CN) networks, Immigration Program Guidance (IPG), Case Management Branch (CMB) and Operations Planning and Performance Branch (OPPB) worked collaboratively with IRCC's Learning Academy to develop this course to support you in your work.

Whether you work in Canada (at a case processing centre or an IRCC local office), or at an office outside Canada, you will find the content of this course relevant to your job. That is because we apply the same Act, Regulations, and guidelines. Albeit differences exist depending on the roles and responsibilities of your office. For that, you will find specific notes and activities in this eWorkbook.

A-2021-22877-000170

nmigration, Refugees Immigration, Ré 1*1 et Citoyenneté C an cizeship Cada Information disclosed under the Access to Information Act L'nfomaon dedlsn

## TR Decision Making

## Course Goal

By the end of the course, you will be able to process temporary resident applications consistent with the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) and the relevant program delivery instructions (PDI).

# Approach

About practice activities This eWorkbook is designed to encourage active learning. Where information exists, such as manuals, policies and functional guidance, you will be asked to find the information and to apply it to the topic. The TR Decision Making course builds upon prerequisite courses that you completed before. You might want to review some information from the prerequisites before you learn new information. Review Your Current Knowledge exercise in the beginning of each unit will help you to recall what you already know about a corresponding topic. If you feel you have forgotten some relevant information, please review the prerequisites to refresh your knowledge. Questions are reflective activities that help you to review your prior knowledge or knowledge of the course material. You do not have to write down your answers. Exercises help you to become familiar with where to find information and how to apply it. Exercises are not tests—the eWorkbook provides information on how and where to find the answers. They are meant to help you practise using the resources and information you'll be using on the job. Exercise Booklet: Exercises are also provided in the separate exercise booklet. There, you can write down your answers for practice activities. The exercise booklet also has blank, lined pages. Use these to make notes or write questions for your instructor. We recommend keeping your exercise booklet open while working with the eWorkbook. The Participant Guide contains scenarios that you will work on during the group learning sessions. For better learning experience, scenario reading and making your notes before the group learning sessions are required in preparation of each group learning session. During the group learning sessions, you will have opportunities to participate in group discussions and activities, ask questions, and benefit from exchange with your peers and instructors. Answers to the scenarios will be sent to you after the group learning sessions.

## TR Decision Making

1. Making Decisions on Temporary Resident Applications Your role as an officer may be to make decisions on applications for clients outside of Canada or for clients in Canada. You may be responsible for issuing a Temporary Resident Visa (TRV), and/or an electronic Travel Authorization (eTA) to foreign nationals outside Canada, or to authorize or extend periods for authorized visits, study or work for persons in Canada. When assessing TR applications, you must be satisfied that the foreign national meets the requirements and is not inadmissible to Canada. Some requirements are general and applicable to all classes of TR applications (visitors, students, workers), while others are specific to each class. For example, all TR applicants must have a valid travel document, however, only students are required to provide a letter of acceptance (LOA). In this section, you will review your role in the decision-making process.
1.1. Legislative Instruments As you learned in the e-Introduction to Immigration course, there are three main classes of TR's: visitors, students, and temporary workers. In each of the following three units, you will delve into the requirements for each class, and practice making decisions. The classes and the corresponding requirements come from the legislative documents guiding the Immigration programs: the IRPA and the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR). The instruments of Delegation and Designation identify who has the authority to make what type of decisions. The operational guidance and instructions to process TR applications are elaborated in PDIs, Program Delivery Updates (PDUs), Operational Bulletins (OBs) and Operational Reminders (ORs). Program Delivery Instructions (PDIs) are official operational instructions released by IRCC. They provide the most up-to-date guidance for processing applications. They help ensure consistent processing and program delivery. The PDIs aim to help officers interpret acts and regulations. Program Delivery Updates (PDUs) are brief announcements to highlight updates to official IRCC PDIs. Operational Bulletins (OBs) are updates to manual only if a manual has not yet been modernized to PDI format, or for one time emergency instructions for operational readiness.

2.1. Case Management Branch Case Management Branch (CMB) provides direction, support, and decision-making on complex, high-profile, sensitive and/or contentious immigration, citizenship and passport cases. CMB is also responsible for managing litigation and applying the Employer Compliance Regime by conducting desk inspections. CMB generally reaches out to managers regarding specific cases. An example would be a case from the minister's office. Your manager could assign you one of these cases and you would work with CMB on the file. For more information, refer to Handling high-profile, complex, sensitive or contentious cases.
2.2. Client Experience Branch The Client Experience Branch (CEB) is a centre of expertise dedicated to understanding and improving the client experience. From time to time you may receive requests from CEB. For example, they may ask you to provide an update on a client's file, or if a client is asking for a reconsideration to a negative decision you have made.
2.3. Immigration Program Guidance Branch Immigration Program Guidance Branch (IPG) provides direction on all aspects of immigration programs, domestically and internationally. Before speaking with your supervisor on sending a request for functional guidance, you should go through all available resources (i.e. PDI, manuals, bulletins, IRPA, etc.).
2.4. Integrity Risk Management Branch Integrity Risk Management Branch (IRMB) is responsible for ensuring the integrity of IRCC's programs and service delivery under the responsibility of the Operations Sector.
2.5. Migration Health Branch Migration Health Branch (MHB) is the centre of expertise for the management of health-related aspects of migration. They deliver health screening and related services under the authority of the IRPA, and deliver the Interim Federal Health Program.

3. Use of Representatives Some people seek advice from different persons or organizations, for example, lawyers, consultants, friends/family or other third parties. Let's take a look at the different type of representatives and what your responsibility is when an application contains a use of representative form.
3.1. Who can be a representative? Any person who gives an immigration advice or represents a client (for a fee or other form of consideration) must be an authorized representative to do so. The representative can act on behalf of the applicant during processing and request information about the progress of the application.

3.2. Use of a Representative Form All foreign nationals who use a representative compensated or uncompensated must submit a Use of a Representative Form (MM 5476). The form discloses the name and contact information of any representative who provides representation or advice at any stage of an application under IRPA.
3.3. Unprofessional or Unethical Behaviour Professional and ethical misconduct means a representative behaves contradictory to their professional or ethical obligations. Examples could include:
- false promises made to the client providing false information to clients about Canada’s immigration processes failing to provide services agreed to between the representative and client violating or attempting to violate a requirement of IRPA or the Regulations being found guilty of an offence that is relevant to the member's suitability to practice knowingly assisting or inducing an employee or agent to violate or attempt to violate a requirement of IRPA or the Regulations As an officer, you should continue to monitor applications received from any representative if there are specific concerns. Apply risk management and due diligence principles for document verification.

4. Travel Documents Travel documents are internationally accepted documents that allow their holders to travel to other countries. In this section you will learn about who requires a travel document, what documents are acceptable for entering Canada, types of unreliable travel documents, and the types of exemptions.
4.1. Who Requires a Travel Document? R52(1)states that a foreign national seeking to become a temporary resident must hold a valid passport, travel document or identity document. That document must be valid for the period authorized for their stay. For more information, refer to OP 16 / ENF 32 / IP 12 Passports and Travel Documents.

4.2. Unreliable Travel Documents The lack or inconsistent use of security features on travel documents, as well as concerns with the process to produce and issue travel documents, can result in situations in which a document is considered insufficiently resistant to counterfeiting and fraudulent use. Such documents threaten the safety and security of Canadians as well as the integrity of the immigration system. As per R50.1, the Minister may designate certain travel documents as unreliable. IRCC maintains a public list identifying unreliable travel documents that do not meet the requirements of_R50(1)or R52(1). The following are not considered travel documents for the purposes ofR50(1)orR52(1):
- any passport issued by Somalia
- non-machine readable passports issued by the Czech Republic
- temporary passports issued by the Republic of South Africa
- provisional passports issued by Venezuela

# 5. Biometrics

Biometrics are the measurement of unique physical characteristics. They significantly reduce the chance that one individual could pose as, or be mistaken for, another and fingerprints are screened against the national repository of criminal records. Their collection aids in deterring, detecting and stopping the entry of those who pose a risk to the health, safety and security of Canadians. They are also a reliable and accurate tool for establishing identity. Biometrics collection allows the Government of Canada to effectively manage identity, facilitate application processing, and simplify entry for travellers with legitimate identities. In this section, you will learn about biometric requirements and exemptions.

For IRCC's authority to collect biometric information, please refer to the Legal references related to Biometrics and Identity Management.

5.1. What Biometrics are Collected? The following information is collected by IRCC from the applicant, at the session where biometrics are enrolled:
- biographic data: name, date of birth, and other personal details of an applicant as listed on the biographic data page of the applicant's passport or travel document
- 10 fingerprints: fingerprints of the applicant, captured electronically during the biometrics collection session, using an electronic fingerprint-capture device. Not everyone is able to give high quality fingerprints, learn more about processing poor quality fingerprints.
- photograph: a digital photograph of the applicant
A-2021-22877-000191

Immigration, Réfugié 1*1 et Citoyenneté Can Information disclosed under the Access to Information Act L'nfoman dds TR Decision Making

5.2. Who Must Provide Biometrics? Biometric collection is mandatory for all foreign nationals, between the ages of 14 and 79 who are:
- applying for a temporary resident visa
- applying for a work permit or a study permit, (excluding U.S. nationals)
- extension of their stay in Canada
- a work or study permit extension
- applying for permanent residence
- claiming refugee or asylum status There is a processing and collection fee that must be paid each time an applicant provides their biometric information unless they are exempt from paying fees.
- All individual applicants pay CAD$85 to provide their biometrics (unless biometric fee exempt). Families applying together pay a maximum total fee of CAD$170. A maximum fee of CAD$255 applies for groups of three or more performing artists and their staff who are applying for a work permit at the same time.
- The biometric fee is non-refundable once the service has been rendered.
5.3. Which Applicants are Exempted from Submitting Biometrics? Biometrics exemptions are listed under R12.2(1) and R12.6, R12.7 andR12.8 of the IRPR. The exemption list includes but is not limited to:
- applicants younger than 14 years or older than 79 years old at the time of their application
- accredited diplomats of other countries and the United Nations, coming to Canada on official travel
- visa-exempt foreign nationals coming to Canada as visitors
- heads of state and heads of government

## 5.4. Where do Foreign Nationals Go to Provide their Biometrics?

For applicants who need to give their biometrics for a TR application, it is best to apply online or in person at a Visa Application Centre (VAC).

- Online applicants must pay the biometrics fee when they submit their application to receive their Biometrics Instruction Letter (BIL) by email within 24 hours. The letter will direct them to a list of biometrics collection service locations.
- Applicants who apply in person at a VAC do not need to wait to receive a biometrics instruction letter. They can submit their application, pay the biometrics collection fee, based on the payment method available at the VAC, and give their biometrics at the same time. Foreign nationals can go to one of these official locations to give their biometrics (fingerprints and photograph):
- outside Canada and the U.S.
- at one of Canada's VAC's worldwide clients may enrol biometrics with or without a BIL
- an office outside Canada in exceptional circumstances
- in the United States
- at one of the Application Support Centres (ASC) clients can only enrol biometrics with a BIL
- at the port of entry
- asylum claimants, and visa-exempt travellers eligible to apply for a work or study permit at the port of entry
A-2021-22877-000193

- in Canada
- at select Service Canada locations for those eligible to make an in-Canada application clients can only enrol biometrics with a BIL
- at IRCC inland domestic office for Asylum claimants that present themselves at an IRCC office clients may enrol biometrics with or without a BIL
For more information, refer to Where to give your fingerprints and photo (biometrics).

5.5. Partial Enrolment Designated officers have the discretion to exempt applicants from providing one or both pieces of biometric information (fingerprints and photo), if it is determined that the collection of biometric information is impossible or not feasible. For more information, refer to Exemption-Impossible or Not Feasible.
5.6. What is the Validity Period of Biometrics for Temporary Residents? With the implementation of the 1 in 10 policy in the temporary residence stream, biometrics can be reused for subsequent temporary residence applications. The validity period is the period during which previously enrolled biometrics may be reused for subsequent temporary residence applications or requests. For example, if a person is applying for a TRV, a study permit, or a work permit, they only need to give their biometrics once every 10 years. They will not have to provide them again until the 10-year period expires. GCMS will automatically associate valid biometrics to a client's application if they are eligible for 1 in 10. Applicants can find out if their biometrics are still valid and when they expire by using the Check Status Tool.

# 5.7. How to Interpret Status and Results?

After the biometric enrollment has been sent to the RCMP, they will return a search result that will advise the officer if the RCMP already has those fingerprints on file in one of three biometric databases. The RCMP checks the fingerprints against their national repository of criminal records, the immigration database and also the legacy refugee claimant database. The status of the sub-activity in GCMS will tell you if the fingerprints were known to the RCMP and also if they were of sufficient quality to complete a search.

The most common statuses are:

- “Received – No reportable trace (NRT)”: the applicant's fingerprints do not match any existing record in the RCMP criminal or immigration databases. There are no admissibility or identity concerns based on the client's fingerprints.
- “Received – IMM": the applicant's fingerprints were submitted previously as part of an immigration application. The RCMP will return the biographic details associated with those fingerprints from their database. If their information is different than the information on file in GCMS the officer should review the records and follow up, as needed. •"Received-CPIC": the applicant's fingerprints are in the national repository of criminal records. The officer must wait for the Biometric Assessment Unit (BAU) to assess the information the RCMP has on file, enter their opinion in GCMS, and update the officer. The officer may also wish to review the previous record and follow up, as needed.
- "Poor quality": the RCMP cannot conduct a search against their databases as the quality of the fingerprints provided was poor. Learn more about processing poor quality fingerprints.

## Key Points to Remember

In this unit, you learned how to situate your role within the TR program and the related operational network. Here are the key points to remember:

- when making a decision on an application, the key question is whether the foreign national meets the requirements for the application category under which they have applied and is not inadmissible
- the Operations Sector includes three networks (CN, DN and IN) with offices across Canada and around the world any person who gives immigration advice or represents a client for a fee or other form of consideration must be an authorized representative to do so
- foreign nationals seeking to become a TR must hold a travel document that must be valid for the period authorized for their stay
- all clients must provide biometrics whether applying for a TRV, study or work permit
- biometrics collection allows the Government of Canada to effectively manage identity, facilitate application processing and simplify entry for travelers with legitimate identities

# Unit 2: Visitor Applications

### About this Unit

In this unit, you will learn how to process TR applications under the visitor class. Foreign nationals from around the globe visit Canada every year. Some require a TRV or an eTA to travel to Canada, while others may be exempt.

In this unit of the eWorkbook and during the virtual session, you will practice assessing applications and making decisions using scenarios and case studies. Although fictitious, the scenarios represent common situations you will encounter as an officer.

Although some content in your eWorkbook applies to specific networks, it will be useful for you to learn about them as there are linkages between your work and those of your colleagues in other networks. For example, TRV applications are processed by officers outside Canada or officers at the Case Processing Center – Ottawa (CPC-O). Electronic travel authorization applications are mainly

## TR Decision Making

Introduction

To begin, do you know who is considered to be a foreign national? A2(1) states: a foreign national is a person who is not a Canadian citizen or a permanent resident, and includes a stateless person.

A Canadian citizen means a citizen referred to in subsection 3(1) of the Citizenship Act and a permanent resident means a person who has acquired permanent resident status and has not subsequently lost that status under section 46 of IRPA These persons, and every person registered as an Indian under the ndian Act do not need a temporary resident visa to come to Canada as they have a right to enter as per subsections 19(1) and 19(2)of IRPA.

As you have learned in e-Introduction to Immigration, there are several reasons why a foreign national comes to Canada. Some of these reasons may be:

- tourism, visiting family or friends
- study
- work temporarily
In this unit, we will focus on foreign nationals wanting to come to Canada as a temporary resident, and more specifically as a visitor.

Do you know what a “temporary resident” is? A “temporary resident" is a foreign national who is legally authorized to enter Canada for a temporary purpose. They hold temporary resident status when they have been found to meet the requirements of the legislation to enter and/or remain in Canada as a visitor, student, worker or temporary resident permit holder. Only foreign nationals physically in Canada hold temporary resident status.

Please take a few minutes to review the legislative references for visitors that you will explore throughout the unit.

Decision Making – Key Steps when Assessing Visitor Applications International Network-Use these five key steps to help you get started with your decision making process when assessing a temporary resident visa application. As we expand on each step, they will also guide you through the learning points of the unit.

STEP 1: Determine if they are a foreign national If a foreign national, proceed to STEP 2. If Canadian Citizen, refer to A19(1) If permanent resident, refer to procedures re. PRTDs. STEP 2: Determine if a TRV or an ETA is required [A11(1), R7(1), R7.1(1)] If a TRV is required, proceed to STEP 3. If TRV exempt, does the foreign national require an eTA? If yes, eTA application online (refer to the section of the eWorkbook covering eTAs). STEP 3: Determine if the foreign national will leave by the end of the period authorized for their stay [R179(b)], holds a valid travel document [R179(c)], and meets the requirements of R30 if they must submit to a medical examination [R179(f)] If satisfied, proceed to STEP 4. If not satisfied, refuse the TRV application. STEP 4: Determine if the foreign national is not inadmissible to Canada [R179(e)] and is not the subject of a declaration made under L22.1(1) [R179(g)] If not inadmissible, proceed to STEP 5. If inadmissible, refuse the TRV application. STEP 5: Make the final decision Approve the TRV application.

1. Temporary Resident Visa & Electronic Travel Authorization

In the e-Introduction to Immigration (CC8200), you learned that the first step is to apply for a visa or for any other document required by the regulations as per A11(1) of the IRPA. A foreign national who seeks to enter or remain in Canada must have the visa or other documents required under the regulations and show that they will leave Canada by the end of their period of authorized stay A20(1)(b). Application before entering Canada A11(1) states “A foreign national must, before entering Canada, apply to an officer for a visa or for any other document required by the regulations. The visa or document may be issued if, following an examination, the officer is satisfied that the foreign national is not inadmissible and meets the requirements of this Act."
## Documents Required Before Entry

R7(1) states “A foreign national may not enter Canada to remain on a temporary basis without first obtaining a temporary resident visa." Obligation on entry

A20(1)(b)states “Every foreign national, other than a foreign national referred to in section 19, who seeks to enter or remain in Canada must establish to become a temporary resident, that they hold the visa or other document required under regulations and will leave Canada by the end of the period authorized for their stay."

You also learned that if a foreign national does not require a TRV as per R7(2), which refers to R190, they may require an eTA as per R7.1(1), unless exempt from this requirement. Note: A foreign national cannot hold a TRV and an eTA. It is either one or the other, unless exempt.

2.2.3 Dual Intent IRPA includes a section about foreign nationals who have dual intent, which means one for temporary residence and one for permanent residence. A22(2) of IRPA addresses this situation by stating the following: “An intention by a foreign national to become a permanent resident does not preclude them from becoming a temporary resident if the officer is satisfied that they will leave Canada by the end of the period authorized for their stay."
A-2021-22877-000213

nigration, Refugees Immigration, Réfugié and Citizenship Canada et Citoyenneté Can Information disclosed under the Access to Information Act

# TR Decision Making

Dual intent is present when a foreign national who has applied or may apply for permanent residence also applies to enter Canada temporarily as a visitor, student or worker. IRPA recognizes that a person may have “dual intent" of immigrating (if permitted to do so) and of abiding by the conditions of temporary entry. Therefore, to qualify for a TRV in cases where there is dual intent, foreign nationals must satisfy you that they can and will leave Canada at the end of the authorized period of stay if their application for permanent residence is not finalized or is refused.

A22(2) reiterates the essential obligation of a TR. In some cases, TRs may never leave Canada because they can become permanent residents without having to leave. There is nothing wrong with this. However, if their TR status were to end or if they were ordered to leave, they must leave Canada even if they have a PR application in progress. To meet the requirements, they must have a genuine intent to enter Canada temporarily in the short term, even if they have a genuine long-term intent to remain permanently.

## Example of dual intent:

The wish to await the outcome of a PR application in Canada may have legitimate reasons, i.e. a family class applicant may have little to return to in their country and therefore prefers to remain close to family members in Canada. Students or temporary workers may not wish to disrupt their studies/employment to return to their homeland while awaiting the outcome of their application for permanent residence.

Note: You are not obliged to extend TR status if there is a PR application in progress. Evaluate the factors to approve or refuse the

request for a TR extension.

For more information, refer to Temporary Residents: Dual Intent.

2.3. Holds a Passport or other Travel Document R179(c): holds a passport or other document that they may use to enter the country that issued it or another country.

A foreign national seeking to become a temporary resident must hold a valid passport or other travel document as per R52(1), unless exempted under R52(2).

The passport must be valid for the duration of their stay. Therefore, you cannot issue a visa or extend status beyond the validity of passport or the travel document.

2.6. Meets Requirements of Medical Examination, if Needed R179(f): meets the requirements of subsections R30(2) and (3), if they must submit to a medical examination under paragraph 16(2)(b) of the Act.

16(2)(b) of IRPA states: Subject to the regulations, the foreign national must submit to a medical examination. ## TR Decision Making

The Act does not differentiate between types of evidence and does not impose any formal rules on admissibility. There are different types of evidence as seen in Unit 3 of the Introduction to Decision Making course.

5.1. Evidence to Support a Temporary Resident Visa or an Extension of Stay as a Visitor

An assessment of the evidence will assess its relevance and reliability and then determine if the evidence is sufficient to establish that the foreign national meets the requirements to be issued a TRV or a Visitor record following an application. Do you need to consider all of the evidence available? Yes!

## TR Decision Making

Once you have identified the evidence, assess its relevance and reliability and then determine if the evidence is sufficient to establish that the foreign national meets the requirements to be issued a TRV or a visitor record following an application.

# Example:

1) A visitor submits a letter from a friend stating that the foreign national is a good person: this is irrelevant as the requirements are not about the personality of the foreign national. Therefore, you would not have to mention this letter.
2) A visitor submits a letter from parents stating they will support their son financially while in Canada. You conclude that the foreign national does not have sufficient funds. You must address this letter because it is material to your conclusion and explain why this letter did not satisfy you.
You will assign weight to the evidence, by assessing them individually, based on the reliability of the source or its content, and by comparison to the entirety of the evidence. Let's look at an example for a temporary resident:

# Example:

A visitor requesting a visitor record extension is submitting proof of funds to demonstrate that they can sustain themselves for the duration of their requested period of stay. On one hand, you may give little weight to a letter from a parent, because the parent has an interest in the outcome of the application. However, if the content of the parent's letter is confirmed with a Notice of Assessment and a letter from the parent's employer, then you would give it more weight.

NoTE: Whenever the applicant's credibility is in question, or there is concern that a document that is submitted is altered or fraudulent, it is imperative that a procedural fairness exchange occur either by a Procedural Fairness Letter or an interview. The designated officer must consider the applicant's responses and determine whether the basis for refusal stands. It is important to know that credibility has to do with the veracity, usually of the person, but could be applied to a document. Reliability is maybe closer to accuracy, neutrality etc. Therefore you could have a credible applicant that provides information that is not reliable. The term credibility is best used where one would not believe something because it is possibly a lie, fraud or misrepresentation.

It is not generally necessary to proceed with procedural fairness for information that is unreliable, but it is (with rare exception) necessary to proceed with procedural fairness if there are credibility concerns.

# TR Decision Making

9.5. Inadmissibility As seen earlier, to extend temporary resident status to a foreign national, they must not be inadmissible. NoTE: If the application has passed eligibility and results from partner agencies have raised admissibility concerns under A34, A35 or A37, stage 2 decision makers are to transfer the application to the Domestic Network's Centre of Expertise in Security Cases for assessment. This procedure only applies to applications submitted in Canada where the applicant or dependant of concern is in Canada. Certain foreign nationals in Canada that are under Visitor status are authorized to study and work in Canada without a study or work permit. These foreign nationals are not considered to be inadmissible if they meet the requirement of studying or working without a permit. You will learn more about these types of foreign nationals in Unit 3 International Student Applications and Unit 4 Temporary Worker Applications.
10. Make a Decision – Extensions R181(2) provides for officers to consider requests for extensions of temporary resident status and to vary conditions of entry. It states that if, following examination, it is established that the foreign national continues to meet the criteria outlined in R179, that an officer shall extend that status. It does not however, set out any specific criteria for granting or refusing an application to extend temporary resident status or to vary or cancel conditions of entry. As a general rule, therefore, the statutory criteria governing admissibility (A34-A42) and the criteria in R179will apply to decisions respecting these two issues. The decision to extend or refuse an application will often require an assessment of positive factors, i.e. those that support an extension and negative factors, i.e. those that support a refusal. It is your responsibility to weigh all factors and to make, on balance, a decision based on the various considerations. Earlier in this unit, you saw what types of evidence could be provided with a visitor application. If a foreign national wishes to extend their stay in Canada, would the evidence be the same or would they be different? A foreign national would need to satisfy you of the reasons why they want to extend their stay. What have they been doing in Canada? Do they have any evidence of what they have been doing? Have their circumstances changed? What are their ties with their home country? Does the foreign national still have a job in their country? Has the foreign national provided evidence that their leave has been extended? Does the foreign national have sufficient funds to support themselves according to the reasons of extension?

You must consider the reasons for which the request for an extension is being made before approving or refusing the application.

Note: When a temporary resident extension document is issued in Canada for a period resulting in a stay in Canada in excess of six

months for a foreign national from a designated country, an Immigration Medical Examination (lME) is normally required, unless the foreign national had passed medicals prior to arriving to Canada and they have not left Canada for six months or more.

10.1. Reject Visitor Extension If the paper application request for extending temporary resident status is incomplete for missing fees or signature, the case processing center returns the application to the foreign national. The application is considered to have never been received, no maintained status is granted, and the foreign national will be considered in status until the original TR document expires.
10.2. Visitor Extension Referral In certain situations, applications may need to be referred because of program integrity issues or in situations where there is a potential refusal based on criminality, security or medical inadmissibility, which could lead to an A44 report and admissibility hearing.
10.3. Visitor Extension Approval If you have determined that the foreign national meets the eligibility and admissibility requirements, approve the visitor extension application.
10.4. Visitor Extension Refusal If you have determined that the foreign national does not meet either the eligibility or admissibility requirements, refuse the TRV application. If the foreign national is still in status, you should:
- remind the foreign national of the expiry date of their current status or document
- explain the consequences of overstaying past that expiry date

# Unit 3: International Student Applications

About this Unit In this unit, you will learn about temporary residents who want to come to Canada, or are in Canada, to study. Foreign students are persons who may obtain TR status and who:

- have been issued study permits, or are authorized by the Regulations (R) to study without study permits.
Foreign students are a valuable part of our Immigration Program. One of the objectives of the IRPA is to facilitate the entry of visitors, students and temporary workers for purposes such as trade, commerce, tourism, international understanding and cultural, educational and scientific activities. Foreign students benefit Canada by bringing cultural enrichment to the Canadian education scene and by helping to diversify the economy and boost the educational system.

#### TR Decision Making

To determine if a foreign national meets the requirements, you will need to assess the evidence presented by the foreign national. In order to do so, you will:

- learn in detail the requirements to study in Canada
- explore the type of evidence required to meet eligibility and admissibility criteria
- practice assessing and making decisions through exercise scenarios
## Objective

At the end of this unit, you will be able to process applications for authorization to study in Canada consistent with the Immigration Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the Immigration Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) and the relevant program delivery instructions (PDI).

### Outline

You will explore information and complete exercises on the following:

- determining if an activity is considered studies
- determining if a study permit is required
- taking a closer look at the designated learning institution
- eligibility and admissibility to be issued a study permit
- making the final decision
# Why?

Studying the material in this eWorkbook will help you to explore and navigate through the policies and legal requirements for international students. Additionally, there are a number of similarities between the other classes of temporary residence; therefore, developing skills to assess student applications will also help you in processing visitor and worker applications.

Introduction

As you saw in the Unit 2 Visitor Applications, A11(1) states that a foreign national must apply for a visa or other document required by the Regulations before entering Canada. This includes a study permit.R9(1)reinforces A11(1) by stating that “a foreign national may not enter Canada to study without first obtaining a study permit". Please take a few minutes to review the legislative references for study permits that you will explore throughout the unit. In e-Introduction to Immigration, you learned about what is considered studies and some of the requirements to study in Canada. You also learned that foreign nationals may not study in Canada unless authorized to do so by the IRPA.

Take a Closer Look at the Designated Learning Institution As you have learned in step 2, if a study permit is required, a foreign national must be accepted to undertake a program of study at a DLI. As per R216(e), the issuance of study permits is limited to foreign nationals who have been accepted to undertake a program of study at an educational institution that is designated to host international students. Therefore, study permit applications, including applications to extend status, must include a letter of acceptance (LOA) issued by a DLI. You will explore LOA's further in step 4.

- foreign nationals who are exempt from the LOA requirement under R219(2)(a) holders of study permits who are eligible to apply to renew their study permits to complete their course or program of study at a non-DLI

4.1.3 Financial Resources A foreign student wanting to study in Canada must prove that they have sufficient funds to support themselves without working in Canada, as per R220.
### This includes:

- paying their yearly tuition
- maintaining themselves and their accompanying family members during their proposed stay in Canada
- being able to pay the transportation costs to and from Canada
Students are required to demonstrate financial sufficiency for only the first year of studies, regardless of the duration of the course or program of studies in which they are enrolled. In other words, a single student entering a four-year degree program with an annual tuition fee of $15,000 must demonstrate funds of $15,000 to satisfy the requirements, and not the full $60,000 which would be required for four years. Officers should be satisfied, however, that the probability of funding for future years does exist i.e., parents are employed, scholarship is for more than one year.

In assessing the adequacy of a student's financial resources, officers may exercise discretion in the documentation they request from applicants. In situations where student applicants generally pose a very low risk regarding funds, officers may choose to limit or waive routine requirements for documentary evidence.

For more information, refer toStudy permits: Assessing the application, specifically the section on financial sufficiency. Use it as a guideline when assessing financial viability.

4.1.4 Certificat d’acceptation du Québec A Certificat d’acceptation du Québec (CAQ) is an authorization from the Government of Quebec that authorizes someone to study in that province. You shall not issue a study permit to a foreign national who intends to study in the province of Quebec if the laws require that the foreign national holds a CAQ R216(3). With few exemptions, all Quebec-bound foreign nationals must submit a CAQ or a confirmation letter from the Ministère de l’Immigration, de la Francisation et de l’Intégration (MIFI) when applying for a study permit. NOTE: A confirmation letter from MIFI is equivalent to the CAQ. For more information about special considerations and CAQ exemptions for students destined to Quebec, refer to_Study permits: Students destined to Quebec.
4.1.5 Passport Foreign students must meet the passport requirements outlined in R52(1). A foreign national who wishes to extend their student status in Canada must hold a passport or travel document that is valid for the length of their proposed stay. A foreign national is not required to have a passport valid for the entire duration of their course of studies, but the validity of the permit cannot go beyond the passport expiry dateR179(c), R181(2)and R183(2)(c).
4.1.6 Custodianship Every unaccompanied minor child (less than 17 years of age at the time of application) in Canada on study permit needs a custodian. All minor applicants for study permit extensions must supply a notarized declaration, one signed by the parents or legal guardians in the country of origin and one signed by the custodian in Canada, stating that arrangements have been made for the custodian to act in place of a parent. You have to be satisfied that adequate arrangements are in place. Custodians should be 19 years of age or older, regardless of the province of destination.

4.2. Are the Requirements for the Issuance of a Study Permit Met? It is important to ensure that the requirements for the issuance of a study permit are met. R216(1) outlines when an officer shall issue a study permit; i.e. if, following an examination, it is established that:
(a) the foreign national applied for the study permit properly
(b) the foreign national will leave Canada by the end of the period authorized for their stay
(c) the foreign national meets the requirements
(d) the foreign national meets the medical requirements R30(2) and (3)
(e) the foreign national has been accepted to undertake a program of study at a designated learning institution

### TR Decision Making

As stated in A11(1) 'A foreign national must, before entering Canada, apply to an officer for a visa or for any other document required by the regulations. The visa or document may be issued if, following an examination, the officer is satisfied that the foreign national is not inadmissible and meets the requirements of this Act’.

4.2.2 Six-month Ban Provision R221 states that a study permit shall not be issued to a foreign national who has engaged in unauthorized work or study in Canada or who has failed to comply with a condition of a permit unless:
(a) a period of six months has elapsed since the cessation of the unauthorized work or study or failure to comply with a condition
(b) the work or study was unauthorized by reason only that the foreign national did not comply with conditions imposed under paragraph 185(a), any of subparagraphs 185(b)(i) to (iii) or paragraph 185(c); or
(c) the foreign national was subsequently issued a temporary resident permit under subsection 24(1) of the Act
When the officer reviews an application, they will first check GCMS to determine if there is anything that would prevent the foreign national from entering. They will verify the status of the foreign national in reviewing case notes. Generally you need to determine

### whether the "six-month ban" on the issuance of a study permit applies.

The lapse of six months would not apply in the case of inland applications because the foreign national would first have to get their status restored prior to being issued a study permit (refer to RestorationR182).

4.3. Referral In certain situations, applications may need to be referred because of program integrity issues or in situations where there is a potential refusal based on criminality, security or medical inadmissibility, which could lead to an A44 report and admissibility hearing. Referral criteria does change frequently so refer to Program Delivery Updates regularly for any changes.
4.4. Assess the Evidence We just covered the eligibility requirements for a study permit. Foreign nationals will need to satisfy you they meet those requirements.

5. Make the Final Decision At this stage, you should have made your decision to approve, refuse or refer. Once your decision is made, you have to document your decision, generate the appropriate documents and inform the applicant.
5.1. Approve If you have determined that the foreign national meets the eligibility requirements and is not inadmissible, approve the study permit application. For more information on processing steps, refer to Study permits: Final decisions.
# 5.2. Refuse

If you have determined that the foreign national does not meet either the eligibility requirements or is inadmissible, refuse the study permit application. Remember that in some cases, a procedural fairness letter should be sent and opportunity to respond given before a final decision can be made.

For more information on procedural fairness, refer toProcedural fairness. For more information on processing steps, refer to Study permits: Final decisions.

5.3. Validity Periods Once you have determined that a student meets the requirements, you should eliminate or at least minimize further transactions with the student. One of the most effective ways to minimize further transactions is to issue long-term study permits. As perR222(1), the validity of a study permit corresponds to the length of the program of studies plus 90 days following program completion, therefore, a study permit becomes invalid 90 days after the day the student completes their course or program of study.

## Key Points to Remember

- as per R9(1), all foreign nationals are required to obtain a study permit for engaging in academic, professional, vocational or other education or training that is more than six months in duration at a DL in Canada, unless exempted a foreign national is exempt from a study permit requirement if they are described as being authorized to study without the issuance of a study permit in R188or A30(2)
- a foreign national can apply for a study permit before entry, on entry or after entry (R213, R214 and R215)
- to be eligible for a study permit, a foreign national needs to meet the general requirements for all temporary residents R179 as well as the specific requirements ofR216 or R217

In some cases, you may need to conduct an interview with the foreign national in person or by phone. In certain situations, you may need to use the services of an interpreter. Remember that the interpreter cannot be a friend or family member of the foreign national. They must be an accredited interpreter. It should also be noted that counsel and representatives cannot act as interpreters. When IRCC is providing an interpreter and is paying for the interpretation services offered to the clients, the department uses the interpreters from the Immigration Refugee Board of Canada (IRB) list of accredited and security-cleared interpreters. Interpretation services at Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) are guided by the Standard Interpretation Service Contractor Clauses and Conditions. For guidelines to conduct an interview and using the services of an interpreter, see Interviews and Interpreters.

For guidelines on the role of a representatives, see Use of Representatives: Counselling Applicants During Interview.

States that an officer shall issue a temporary resident visa to a foreign national if, following an examination, it is established that the foreign national:

a) applied for a temporary resident visa as a member of the visitor, worker or student class;
b) will leave Canada by the end of the period authorized for their stay;

e) is not inadmissible; and
f) meets the medical requirements.

Ch_01_04_01_A_01 EXERCISE: What Documents are Acceptable for Entering Canada? - Answers As per R52(1), a foreign national seeking to become a temporary resident must hold one of the following documents that is valid for the period authorized for their stay:

(a) a passport that was issued by the country of which the foreign national is a citizen or national, that does not prohibit travel to Canada and that the foreign national may use to enter the country of issue;
(b) a travel document that was issued by the country of which the foreign national is a citizen or national, that does not prohibit travel to Canada and that the foreign national may use to enter the country of issue;
(c) an identity or travel document that was issued by a country, that does not prohibit travel to Canada, that the foreign national may use to enter the country of issue and that is of the type issued by that country to non-national residents, refugees or stateless persons who are unable to obtain a passport or other travel document from their country of citizenship or nationality or who have no country of citizenship or nationality;
(d) a laissez-passer that was issued by the United Nations;
(e) a passport or travel document that was issued by the Palestinian Authority;
(f) a document that was issued by the Organization of American States and is entitled “Official Travel Document”;
(g) a passport issued by the United Kingdom to a British Overseas Citizen;
(h) a passport issued by the United Kingdom to a British National (Overseas), as a person born, naturalized or registered in Hong Kong;
(i) a passport issued by the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China; or
(j) a passport issued by the United Kingdom to a British Subject.

Ch_01_04_02_A_01 EXERCISE: Who is Exempt from Having a Valid Travel Document to Enter Canada as a TR? - Answers As per R52(2), the following foreign nationals are exempt from the requirement of passports, travel document or identity documents:

(a) citizens of the United States;
(b) persons seeking to enter Canada from the United States or St. Pierre and Miquelon who have been lawfully admitted to the United States for permanent residence;
(c) residents of Greenland seeking to enter Canada from Greenland;
(d) persons seeking to enter Canada from St. Pierre and Miquelon who are citizens of France and residents of St. Pierre and Miquelon;
(e) members of the armed forces of a country that is a designated state for the purposes of the Visiting Forces Act who are seeking entry in order to carry out official duties, other than persons who have been designated as a civilian component of those armed forces;
(f) persons who are seeking to enter Canada as, or in order to become, members of a crew of a means of air transportation and who hold an airline flight crew licence or crew member certificate issued in accordance with International Civil Aviation Organization specifications; or
(g) persons seeking to enter Canada as members of a crew who hold a seafarer's identity document issued under International Labour Organization conventions and are members of the crew of the vessel that carries them to Canada.

## TR Decision Making

CH_01_05_05_A_01 EXERCISE: Biometrics – Answers

1. An applicant, that turned 14 years old after her application was submitted, is required to provide biometrics. True or False? This is false because the biometric requirement is based on the age the applicant at the time of application.
2. The RCMP returns the response Received – CPIC in response to Tina's biometric enrollment. A match for her fingerprints has been found in the immigration database. True or False? “Received – CPIC” means that the applicant's fingerprints are in the national repository of criminal records. Therefore, this is false. Received — IMM means that the applicant's fingerprints were submitted previously to the RCMP as part of an immigration application.
3. Harpreet is applying for a study permit and needs to submit biometrics as he has never applied to come to Canada before. True or False? True. As of December 31, 2018, nationals of India are required to provide their biometrics in support of a TR, PR, and REF-CLM. Should nationals of India have an outstanding application submitted before December 31st 2018, they are biometrically exempt. The exemption is based on the date IRCC's received the application (i.e. Rec'd Date).
4. Even though Juan has provided his biometrics within the last 10 years for a previous TR application, he is required to submit new biometrics for his new TR application. True or False? With the implementation of the 1 in 10 policy in the temporary residence stream, biometrics can be re-used for subsequent temporary residence applications. This is false because the applicant provided his biometrics within the last ten years, therefore his biometrics can be used for his subsequent TR application as it is still valid.

5. Designated officers have the discretion to exempt applications from providing one or both pieces of biometric information.
#### True or False?

This is true. Designated officers have the discretion to exempt applicants from providing one or both pieces of biometric information (fingerprints and photo), if it is determined that the collection of biometric information is impossible or not feasible.

# Unit 2: Visitor Applications

CH_02_01_00_A_01 REVIEW YOUR CURRENT KNOWLEDGE: TRV or eTA-Answers

1. The foreign nationals should submit their application either online or to the office outside Canada that is responsible for serving the country in which they have been lawfully admitted or their country of nationality. For more information, refer to the list of countries and corresponding offices.
2. Paragraph 7(2) of IRPA states the foreign nationals who are exempted from obtaining a temporary resident visa. R7(2)(a) states that a temporary resident visa requirement does not apply to a foreign national who is exempted under Division 5 of Part 9 of the regulations. This refers directly to R190(1), R190(2), R190(2.1), R190(3), R190(3.1) which identify the foreign nationals that are exempt from the requirement to obtain a TRV.
- R190(1) identifies those that are exempt based on nationality
- R190(2) identifies those that are exempt based on documents •R190(3)identifies those that are exempt based on purpose of entry
3. Yes. Foreign nationals that are visa-exempt are required to obtain an eTA before travelling to Canada by air, unless otherwise exempted from the requirement.
4. No, there are foreign nationals that are exempt from both a TRV and an eTA such as US citizens and foreign nationals travelling in or transiting through Canada by land, sea, or rail. For more information, refer toR7.1(2), (3). These paragraphs describe the foreign nationals who are exempt from the eTA requirement.

# TR Decision Making

5. Foreign nationals need to apply online using the Come to Canada Wizard. The eTA is an automated process if there are no concerns. If there are concerns (ex. criminality), the eTA will drop out of the automated process and will go for review with an officer at OSC or to an office outside Canada if local information is required.
6. An eTA is valid for five years or until foreign national's passport expires, whichever comes first. An eTA can also be cancelled by a designated officer. Once cancelled, the eTA is no longer valid.

7. eTA applications fall out of the automated process and are referred to an officer for the following reasons:
- Identity reconciliation
- Derogatory information
- eTA application hits against the Lost, Stolen and Fraudulent Document Database
- Canadian citizen or permanent resident
- Adverse information on file

For more information, refer to manually processing electronic travel authorization applications section.

(b) will leave Canada by the end of the period authorized for their stay under Division 2;
(c) holds a passport or other document that they may use to enter the country that issued it or another country;
(d) meets the requirements applicable to that class;
(e) is not inadmissible;

WhatQuestions_Consider_A EXERCISE: What Questions Would You Consider-Answers There are several factors to consider when assessing a TRV or a request to extend a TR stay. i.e. criminality, employment, refugee claim, touring, visiting relatives, etc. Are the plans well thought, considering their circumstances back in their home country?
Reason(s) for the request

i.e. One more month to see snow might be reasonable but is six months? Did the foreign national already experience winter in Canada?

Location of dependants Is the whole family in Canada or are there spouse/children to go back to in their home country?

## TR Decision Making

EXERCISE: Authorized Period of Stay-Answers R183(4) - The period authorized for a temporary resident's stay ends on the earliest of

(a) the day on which the temporary resident leaves Canada without obtaining prior authorization to re-enter Canada;
(b) the day on which their permit becomes invalid, in the case of a temporary resident who has been issued either a work permit or a study permit;
(c) the day on which any temporary resident permit issued to the temporary resident is no longer valid under section 63;
(d) the day on which the period authorized under subsection (2) ends, if paragraphs (a) to (c) do not apply.
R183(5) – If a TR has applied for an extension of the period of authorized stay and a decision is not made on the application by the end of the period authorized for their stay, the period is extended until

(a) the day on which a decision is made, if the application is refused; or
(b) the end of the new period authorized for their stay, if the application is allowed.

No Medical Exam Required

(a) all foreign nationals other than those listed under R30(1)(a)(i) to (vi).

(c) a family member of a person described in paragraph 186(b), unless that family member seeks to engage or continue in employment in Canada.

## TR Decision Making

Answer 5:

1) Reasonable grounds to believe: If there are reasonable grounds to believe that a foreign national may be inadmissible under A38(1), an officer may request a medical examination. (i.e. information in the file shows they may have a mental illness that might be a danger to the safety). Reasonable grounds to believe means that the officer has more than a mere suspicion. The officer must have more facts to be able to conclude that there are reasonable grounds to believe.
2) Persons who are applying for a Super visa
## 3) Some temporary residents seeking medical treatment in Canada

Answer 6: If a foreign national plans to visit Canada for six months or less, a medical examination is not required unless the foreign national intends to work in an occupation in which the protection of public health is essential and you don't have reasonable grounds to

# believe that the foreign national may be medically inadmissible.

## Answer 7:

As per R30(1)(a) (iii), foreign nationals seeking to come to Canada for more than six months require a medical examination if they have resided in a designated country for six consecutive months or more within the year preceding the date of their application

## (what we call the 6 + 6 Rule).

NoTE: The designated country is the country where the foreign national has resided six months or more. It is not necessarily where they are nationals. Medical examination is also required for:

- Foreign nationals who are seeking to work in occupations in which the protection of public health is essential, regardless of the length of stay
- Foreign nationals who you have reasonable grounds to believe are inadmissible under A38(1), as perR30(1)(a)(iv), regardless of the length of stay

Based on the information above, are you satisfied with the evidence to make a decision? Explain. Yes, I am satisfied with the evidence to make a decision.

- Admissibility — There is not enough evidence to write an A44 report. Admissibility passed.

- Approve extension valid to the day before passport expiry date
- Refuse as Baylor does not need to be in Canada to await for spousal decision, have concerns about employment overseas and possible credibility concerns

REVIEW YOUR CURRENT KNOWLEDGE: Status—Answers Answer 1:

There are three ways that a temporary resident can lose their status in Canada as per A47.

As you have learned in the e-Introduction to Immigration, a foreign national loses temporary resident status at per A47:

(a) At the end of the period for which they are authorized to remain in Canada;
(b) On a determination by an officer or the Immigration Division that they have failed to comply with any other requirement of this Act; or
(c) On cancellation of their temporary resident permit.
If a foreign national is not in status, then they are in violation of A29(2)and are therefore inadmissible under A41(a)—non- compliance. A temporary resident is responsible for leaving Canada by the end of the period authorized for their stay.

## Answer 2:

The three different ways that a decision can be communicated to the foreign national when entering Canada are:

1) By verbal authorization
2) By stamping the passport
3) By issuing a Visitor Record
If there is no stamp in the passport and the foreign national has not been issued a Visitor record, the entry date can be verified by doing a query using the Entry/Exit tab in GCMS. When entering Canada, the passports are scanned electronically (PIK Process).

For more information, refer to Automated ports of entry.

## TR Decision Making

EXERCISE: Restoration Overview—Answers

Answer 1: The eligibility requirements for restoration are:

- apply within 90 days of having lost their status meet the initial requirements for their stay remain in Canada until a decision is made have not failed to comply with any condition imposed automatically by regulation [R183] or by an officer [R185], other than those stated below
- have lost their status only because they have failed to comply with any of the following conditions imposed by an officer: the period authorized for their stay—R185(a) the work that they are permitted to engage in, or are prohibited from engaging in, in Canada—R185(b)(i) to (iii),
including the type of work, employer and location of work 。 the studies that they are permitted to engage in, or are prohibited from engaging in, in Canada—R185(c), including the type of studies, educational institution, location or times and periods of the studies

- continue to meet the requirements of a temporary resident and the requirements of the work or study permit, as applicable
Answer 2: A foreign national who has applied to restore their status has lost their status and may not continue to work or study until their status has been restored and a new work permit or study permit has been issued.

Answer 3: No. If a foreign national leaves Canada during the process of their application to restore their status, the officer must refuse the application as they are no longer eligible to apply for restoration.
